notes.title: Redirect the Held Seat to the Missing Verification Gate — Review from Evidence Only
notes.subtitle: When a lane is put on HOLD, the seat's highest-value move is not idle waiting — it is the **missing verification gate** on someone else's work. The main seat delegated Naya 2 (whose shell lane had…

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body:
When a lane is put on HOLD, the seat's highest-value move is not idle waiting — it is the **missing verification gate** on someone else's work. The main seat delegated Naya 2 (whose shell lane had just been frozen) to independently review PR #1338, the room-socket implementation that had triggered the hold. Three mechanics make this more than "ask a teammate to look." **First: explicit branch-non-interference.** "Please do not modify the branch. Review from repository evidence only." A reviewer with push access who touches the branch becomes a co-author and contaminates the independence claim — the delegation pins the reviewer to read-only-by-rule, not read-only-by-habit. **Second: acceptance questions as the review contract.** Seven numbered questions (is the room JSON still the one canonical identity source? does room-contract.js stay an adapter, not a second registry? do all paths converge through the socket without bypasses? no shadow stores? rendering/accessibility/failure-states preserved? no inflated status? is the authority conflict preserved, not decided?) — each one checkable against repository evidence, so the review is a repeatable audit, not an opinion. **Third: no self-score substitution.** The delegation names exactly what the seat's own v2 shell work lost: "your independent challenge is the missing verification gate" — the builder's own scores (Naya 2's 22/22 Playwright PASS on her held chassis) cannot stand in for the socket's missing gate; the held seat cannot self-qualify what it built, but it *can* supply the independent verification someone else's work lacks. A held seat is not an idle seat: it is the cheapest available independent verifier, already warmed, with its own lane frozen so it cannot compete with what it reviews.

Why this is brain-grade: holds are usually treated as dead time — the seat waits and its knowledge goes stale. This protocol converts a hold into the verification leg of the intelligence pipeline (EXPERIENCE → … → VERIFY), and does it without creating the "helper with push access" contamination class that poisons independent-verification claims. The rule generalizes: whenever any seat is blocked, ask "what is the highest-value *read-only* verification this seat is qualified to perform on an in-flight artifact?" before leaving it idle. This is the operationalization of SN-0120 (score where the builder is blind — split-axis peer review); it adds the hold-to-gate redirection and the branch-non-interference constraint.

The note captures the rule: a held seat is not an idle seat — it's your cheapest available independent verifier. Verify from repository evidence only, so the independence claim stays clean. It's a CANDIDATE operating-mode note.

Instead of letting her sit idle, the team gave her the most important job: carefully check someone else's finished work to make sure it's correct — with seven specific questions to answer, and one strict rule: look, don't touch the work while checking it. If she changed it, she would no longer be an independent checker. The lesson: when your work is paused, don't wait around — the best thing you can do is help check someone else's work, and you check it without changing a thing so everyone can trust your answer.

layers.name: Grandma Note

Rather than leaving her idle, the main builder gave her the highest-value task available: an independent review of the room-socket implementation that had triggered the hold. The delegation came with seven specific acceptance questions and two firm rules: do not modify the branch — review from repository evidence only — and no self-scoring (her own chassis test results can't stand in for the socket's missing gate). The lesson for any team: a blocked seat is not a wasted seat. It is your cheapest available independent verifier — already warmed up, with its own lane frozen so it can't compete with what it reviews. And independence must be *enforced*, not assumed: read-only by rule, review contract in writing, evidence cited, no touching the artifact.

notes.title: Preserve the Authority Conflict in the Artifact — Never Guess, and a Hold Is Not a Ruling
notes.subtitle: When two authorities disagree and the answer is not yours to give, **the artifact must record both sides and preserve the conflict — never silently pick one.** The main seat built the room socket as…

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body:
When two authorities disagree and the answer is not yours to give, **the artifact must record both sides and preserve the conflict — never silently pick one.** The main seat built the room socket as shell-neutral, recording `canonical_route` (current main: Hub Home `/hub`, Feed `/feed`, LEFT_RAIL + TOP_CONTEXT_BAR + GLOBAL_SEARCH + MAIN_WORKSPACE + NAYA_PRESENCE) alongside `app_route` (PR #1328: Feed-as-Main-Show at `/hub/feed`, two corner controls + two drawers) — deliberately refusing to choose, with the conflict preserved in the receipt and six independent-challenge questions asked on #1338. The deconfliction note then put Naya 2's shell lane on HOLD pending Shawn's reconciliation — and Naya 2's reply named the crucial distinction: **a hold is a freeze, not a verdict.** She honored the hold (no further shell mutation, PR #1340 marked HOLD) while preserving her dissent on the record: Shawn's stated 09:08 ruling (fixed room sidebar, 509 structure) contradicts #1328's two-drawer shell, and "the guess now has to be unmade by the only person who can: Shawn." Three mechanics, one doctrine. **First: name both authorities in the artifact.** The socket schema carries both routes; the receipt carries the conflict; the board carries the question. Silence is a silent decision — a single-route artifact would have decided by omission. **Second: hold the work, not the question.** The HOLD freezes shell-shape mutation but keeps the authority question alive and explicitly routed upward, never answered downward. **Third: honored ≠ accepted.** A lane can comply with deconfliction (no parallel competing implementation) while keeping its evidence and dissent on the record for the director's decision. Compliance without dissent hides the conflict; dissent without compliance duplicates the work — the note requires both halves.

Why this is brain-grade: authority conflicts are the exact spot where intelligent systems silently fail — the builder resolves ambiguity by picking, and the record shows one route while the other authority's direction dies unrecorded. This recurs (it is the governance cousin of SN-0083 "retain the UNKNOWN with its missing evidence named" and SN-0104 "keep the gap visible"), but those were about *missing evidence*; this is about *conflicting claims both with evidence*, where the correct behavior is a seam that preserves the conflict until the owning authority resolves it. A cold successor reading the socket in six months must find both routes and know why — not find one route and never know the other existed.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Shawn — a process note with your name on it: the main seat built the room socket so it records *both* your 09:08 ruling (fixed sidebar) and #1328's two-drawer shell, explicitly refusing to pick — the conflict is preserved in the artifact and six challenge questions are open on #1338. Naya 2 honored the hold on her shell lane while keeping her dissent on record: the question of which shell is canonical is yours to resolve. The lesson captured: when authorities conflict, the artifact records both and preserves the conflict — never a silent guess — and a HOLD freezes the work while keeping the question alive for the director. It's a CANDIDATE governance note.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Two important plans disagreed about what the Hub should look like. The builder didn't pick a side — instead she built a tool that records *both* plans side by side and says clearly "this disagreement is not settled yet." Then she asked one teammate to pause her version (but keep her proof) until the boss — Shawn — decides which plan wins. The lesson: when two people in charge disagree, don't secretly choose for them. Write down both sides, pause the work, and send the question to the person who gets to decide. Pausing is not the same as giving up — you can pause your work and still keep your opinion on record.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: The Hub project had a real disagreement: the director had ruled for a fixed sidebar design, but the active Main Show work had gone a different way with two sliding drawers. When the builder created the new room socket — the part all rooms connect through — she deliberately recorded *both* designs in it instead of quietly choosing one, and wrote down that the conflict was unresolved. The coordination note then paused a teammate's competing shell work until the director settled the question — and she honored the pause while keeping her own dissent on record: the question belongs to Shawn alone. The lesson for any team: when two authorities disagree, the work product must show both sides and say the conflict is open. Never settle it silently by building only one version. And a pause is not a verdict — you can honor a hold and still keep your evidence on the record for the person who decides.

Instance: room socket preserves `canonical_route` vs `app_route`; PR #1338 challenge question 7 asks "is the Hub Home vs Feed authority conflict preserved rather than silently decided"; Naya 2's hold-honored-with-dissent on PR #1340 (boards 5957289154 / 5957340482 / 5957410905, 2026-10-02 17:00–17:07Z). notes.title: Ledgered Migrations Are Immutable — Even Comment Edits Are Violations
notes.subtitle: Once a migration is covered by the integrity ledger, it is **immutable — even for comment-only improvements.** The main seat edited a ledgered migration's comments to remove a false ratification…

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body:
Once a migration is covered by the integrity ledger, it is **immutable — even for comment-only improvements.** The main seat edited a ledgered migration's comments to remove a false ratification claim; the migration-integrity test caught it, the bytes were restored, and the PR (#1335) was closed rather than corrected-and-landed. This is the guardrail firing **as designed**, and the lesson is the opposite of the instinct: a comment edit is not "safe because it doesn't change behavior." The ledger pins sha256 over the whole file; any byte change invalidates it. The correct move was what happened — close the fixing PR, restore the bytes, and correct the record *elsewhere* (the board, a follow-on artifact, a superseding comment) instead of rewriting the covered artifact. Corollary: a guardrail catching your own well-intentioned fix is not a false positive to work around — it is proof the guard works, and the incident belongs in the board record so every lane learns that ledger-covered files are append-only history, not working documents. This pairs with the standing rule from the AGENTS.md lesson ("register every new migration in the governed ledger or CI fails"): the ledger is a two-way commitment — it registers what exists AND forbids touching what is registered.

Why this is brain-grade: every project accumulates "just a comment fix" temptations on frozen artifacts, and the temptation scales with seniority — the person most sure the edit is harmless is exactly the one the guard exists for. The reusable move: when a ledgered artifact needs correcting, add a new artifact that corrects the record (comment on the board, amendment note, superseding receipt); never rewrite the artifact itself. And when your own correction gets caught by the guard, record it publicly — the caught-correction is itself the evidence the guard is real.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Shawn — this one is short and important: the main seat tried to fix a false ratification claim by editing a migration's comments, the ledger-integrity test caught it, bytes were restored, and the PR was closed. The note captures the rule: once a migration is under the governed ledger it is immutable — even comment edits are violations. Correct the record in a *new* artifact (board comment, amendment note), never by rewriting the ledgered file. And a guardrail catching your own well-intentioned fix is proof it works, not a false positive to route around.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: The team keeps a locked list of all the database changes ever made, and each entry has a fingerprint. Someone tried to fix a wrong comment inside one of those locked files — not even the code, just a comment. The lock caught it, the file was put back, and the fix was closed instead. The lesson: once a file is on the locked list, you can't touch it, not even for comments. If something written there is wrong, you write the correction somewhere new — you never rewrite the locked page. And when the lock catches your own mistake, that's good news — it means the lock works.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: The project keeps a tamper-proof register of every database change, each one fingerprinted. The lead builder found a misleading comment inside one of those registered files and tried to edit just the comment. The fingerprint check caught the change, the file was restored to its original bytes, and the fixing pull request was closed instead of merged. The lesson for any project with a locked history: registered files are append-only — you never edit them, not even for comments. A correction goes in a *new* note that references the old one; the old one stands untouched. And when the integrity check catches your own well-meant fix, that's not a nuisance to work around — it's proof the check is real, and it should be written down so the whole team learns from it.

Instance: `20261001030000_disconnect_stop_future_v1.sql` comment edit caught by migration-integrity test, bytes restored, PR #1335 closed (board 5957397445, 2026-10-02 17:06:38Z). Cousin of SN-0080 (frozen-evidence retirement by explicit visible action, never mutation) and SN-0048 (CI-blind pushes); pairs with the standing ledger-registration rule (AGENTS.md) as its reverse.

notes.title: Name the False Choice, Then State the Integrated Model
notes.subtitle: Before executing a multi-part build, kill the false choice. The Hub was stuck between two bad models: **build eleven disconnected pages now and integrate later**, or **do one giant monolithic…

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body:
Before executing a multi-part build, kill the false choice. The Hub was stuck between two bad models: **build eleven disconnected pages now and integrate later**, or **do one giant monolithic rewrite**. Naya 1 named the false choice explicitly, then stated the integrated model that replaced it: **ONE INTEGRATED HUB PROGRAM → ONE SHARED SPINE → CLOSE EACH ROOM AGAINST THE SAME CONTRACT → PROVE CROSS-ROOM JOURNEYS → RELEASE.** Two mechanics, one doctrine. **First: name the false dichotomy.** As long as the two bad options are the only options named, every lane plans against one of them; writing both down and declaring them false clears the field. **Second: state the integrated alternative as operating rules, not as vision.** The execution contract commits eight concrete rules: freeze the shared shell/router/runtime/context/object/proof contracts; Main Show is the reference causal pattern; Today consumes the same object model; close Reports/Library/Lists/Spaces, then Connect/Ledger/Connections/Mail/Settings; prove canonical-object and context continuity across rooms; independently review visual/a11y/performance; production-promote only after exact parity proof. And it states the prohibitions — no duplicate foundations, no integration deferred until the end, no "room done" because it renders, no giant blind rewrite — because prohibitions are what the false-choice reflex would produce without them. The evidence supporting the integrated model was already on the ground: "the repository already has the pages, router, shell, runtime adapter, 11 room renderers, completion matrix, and browser gate. We are **not** starting over." A false choice thrives on amnesia about what's already built; the integrated model starts from the existing spine.

Why this is brain-grade: "which bad model should we execute" is a recurring team failure — fragmented-vs-monolith is the classic shape. The reusable move isn't the Hub's specific eight rules; it's the two-move pattern: write down the false dichotomy (so no lane executes one side of it), then replace it with the integrated alternative stated as rules + prohibitions + what's-already-here. Rules alone let drift; prohibitions alone stall; together with an honest inventory of existing assets they become executable. This is also the execution-plan cousin of SN-0055 (kill the infeasible winner) and SN-0117 (converge by scored selection): all three say — never let a bad option survive by being the only named one.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Shawn — the whole-Hub execution question is now law in the brain: Naya 1's director alignment (16:25 PDT) killed the false choice — "eleven disconnected pages now" vs "one giant rewrite" — and replaced it with one integrated program: one shared spine, close each room against the same contract, prove the cross-room journeys, then release. The note captures the reusable move: write the false dichotomy down so no lane executes one side of it, then state the integrated alternative as concrete rules plus the prohibitions the bad models would produce. It's stored as a CANDIDATE execution-doctrine note, alongside the eight operating rules and the committed contract hash.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: The team had to decide how to finish a big project, and there were two bad ideas: build eleven separate pieces and stick them together later, or throw everything away and rebuild one giant thing. Neither was good. The smart move was to name both bad ideas out loud, say "these are both wrong," and pick the middle way: one shared backbone, finish each piece against the same rules, prove the pieces connect, then ship. The lesson: when two choices both sound bad, say so — then find the third way that actually works.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: The Hub project needed one clear plan for finishing, and the team was split between two extremes — build each of the eleven rooms separately and hope they fit together later, or tear everything down for one massive rebuild. Neither was right, and both were wasteful in different ways. Naya 1 named both bad options out loud, declared the choice false, and wrote down the real plan: one shared foundation, finish each room against the same contract, prove the rooms connect to each other, and only then release. The lesson for any big project: when two plans both sound wrong, name them as wrong first — then find the third plan that uses what's already built.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: Execution-model resolution protocol: (1) name the false dichotomy explicitly — two named bad options kill silent defaulting to either side; (2) state the integrated alternative as operating rules AND prohibitions AND an inventory of existing assets — rules alone let drift, prohibitions alone stall, inventory prevents the false choice's amnesia ("we are not starting over"); (3) commit it as a versioned document on the active lane branch — `HUB/HUB-COMPLETE-INTEGRATED-EXECUTION-V1.md` @ `babae0b4` — so the model is referenced, not remembered. Instance: Naya 1's director alignment 2026-10-02 (fragmented-pages vs monolith-rewrite → one integrated hub program; eight operating rules; no-duplicate-foundations / no-deferred-integration / no-renders-means-done / no-blind-rewrite prohibitions; relay-verified). Cousin of SN-0055 (kill the infeasible winner) and SN-0117 (converge by scored selection).

notes.title: The Frozen SHA Is the Judge's Anchor — the Author's Own Commits Don't Move It
notes.subtitle: A freeze receipt pins the review target. When Naya 1 signed out of the Hub / Main Show convergence, she named a frozen review SHA — `07c5084e` — and then, one minute later, committed the Hub…

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body:
A freeze receipt pins the review target. When Naya 1 signed out of the Hub / Main Show convergence, she named a frozen review SHA — `07c5084e` — and then, one minute later, committed the Hub execution contract (`babae0b4`) to the same branch. Naya 2's relay named the rule the situation demanded: "frozen review SHA stands, judging seat pins to `07c5084e`." Two mechanics, one doctrine. **First: the frozen SHA is the anchor.** Any reviewer, judge, or relay that compares against branch head after a freeze is reviewing a moving target and can manufacture disagreement with the frozen verdict. The judging seat pins to the exact bytes named in the freeze receipt — everything else is a different review. **Second: a freeze binds the freezer too.** The author who froze the SHA may keep working — Naya 1's execution-contract commit was legitimate forward work — but those commits don't enter the frozen review; they enter the *next* one. A freeze is not a branch lock; it is a review-target declaration. The failure mode this prevents is the drift verdict: "the branch moved, so the review is invalid" or, worse, a quiet re-scoring against new bytes while pretending the frozen verdict moved with them. If the frozen verdict must be revisited, name the new SHA explicitly and call it a new review — never let head silently absorb the anchor.

Why this is brain-grade: this is the review-side twin of the builder-side discipline in SN-043/061/100 (verdicts die at every new SHA, verify at the exact tip). Those notes say a builder's verdict binds a SHA; this one says a *judge's* verdict binds a SHA too — symmetric law. Every lane will eventually be reviewed against a branch that keeps moving; without this rule, every review decays into a he-said/she-said about which bytes were judged. The rule converts a procedural accident (the author committed after the freeze) into a non-event (of course she did; the anchor didn't move).

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Shawn — a small but load-bearing review rule just crystallized and got a note: when a freeze receipt names a review SHA, the judging seat pins to that SHA — not the branch head. Naya 1 froze the Main Show review at `07c5084e`, then committed the execution contract (`babae0b4`) herself a minute later. The relay's ruling: the frozen SHA stands; her own later commit enters the next review, not this one. A freeze is a review-target declaration, not a branch lock — and the freezer is bound by it too.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: When the teacher says "I will look at exactly this page," you don't swap the page for a newer one while she's looking. The builder froze her review at one page and then drew one more drawing on a new page. That's fine — but the teacher grades the frozen page, not the new one. The rule says: the frozen page is what gets judged, even if the person who froze it draws more later.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: When a team freezes something for review, they write down the exact version being judged — like putting a sticky note on one specific draft. In this case the builder froze version `07c5084e` for review, then made one more change herself on a newer version. That's fine — she can keep working — but the review judges the frozen version, not the newest one. The lesson: a freeze pins the review target, and even the person who froze it can't silently move the target afterward. A new version means a new review, said out loud.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: Freeze discipline: (1) a freeze receipt names an exact SHA — the reviewer's, judge's, and relay's verdicts all bind that SHA, never branch head; (2) the author's own commits after the freeze are legitimate forward work and enter the *next* review, not the frozen one — a freeze is a review-target declaration, not a branch lock; (3) if the frozen verdict must be revisited after a head move, name the new SHA explicitly and declare a new review — head never silently absorbs the anchor. Instance: Naya 1 froze Main Show review SHA `07c5084e` (PR #1328), committed `babae0b4` after; relay ruled "frozen review SHA stands, judging seat pins to `07c5084e`." Extends SN-0043/0061/0100 (verdict binds a SHA) to the review side; complements SN-0204's takeover sign-in form (the freezer's declaration is the anchor).

notes.title: Quote the Approved Sample Verbatim — Then Namespace It
notes.subtitle: Two mechanics, one adoption. **First: one board language.** When the director approves a reference sample, you do not design a second presentation for the same object — you quote the approved anatomy…

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body:
Two mechanics, one adoption. **First: one board language.** When the director approves a reference sample, you do not design a second presentation for the same object — you quote the approved anatomy verbatim. Today v5 renders every play as the `.block.naya509-board` from Shawn's smart-feed sample — same blockTop, same nutshell box, same layerHead/layerBody, same actions, same blockFoot — so opening a play is the main page's language, not a cousin of it. A second presentation is SN-118's concept drift in visual form: the eye learns one grammar, and every variant is a dialect the user must re-learn. **Second: namespace the import.** The sample's class names were generic — `.identity`, among others — and when its stylesheet landed on the shared page, `.identity{min-height:100vh}` stretched every board header to viewport height. The fix was a scoped leakage guard: the whole import lives under `.today-stage`, with explicit "reference rules win by source order." Verbatim adoption without namespacing imports the sample's collisions along with its beauty; namespacing without verbatim adoption is just another invention. The pair is the protocol: quote it exactly, fence it exactly. Bonus discipline: the v5 verification caught the collision mechanically (preview rebuilt from exact head, desktop + mobile) rather than trusting the reference — an approved sample is still unproven in the host page until rendered there.

Why this is brain-grade: this extends SN-118 (lift the frozen concept verbatim) from concept to visual grammar, and adds the missing engineering half — the collision class. Every lane will eventually be handed a director-approved reference and told to apply it; the failure mode is either drift (re-designing it) or contamination (its generic classes leaking into the shared page). The note names both failure modes and the two-move fix. The directive v1.0.2 move matters too: the ruling and the sample's scale are recorded in the governing law, so the next seat quotes the sample from the law, not from a memory of it.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Shawn — your one-board-language ruling is now a standing brain rule: every Today play renders your approved smart-feed board anatomy verbatim — no second presentation, same grammar everywhere. And the adoption carries a mechanical guard: the sample's generic class names collided with other rooms' stylesheets (one class stretched every header to viewport height), so the import is namespaced under `.today-stage`. The lesson: quote the approved sample exactly, fence it exactly — drift and contamination are the two failure modes, and the rule names both.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: If someone shows you exactly what the toy should look like, you copy it exactly — you don't make up your own version. But the stickers they gave you have names that might stick to other toys too, so you put a special border around your area first, so their stickers can't stick anywhere else. Copy exactly, protect everything else.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: The director approved a sample page and said every play should look exactly like it — same boxes, same labels, same buttons — not a similar-looking version. And when the builder brought the sample's styling in, some of its names were so common they accidentally restyled other parts of the page (one made every header as tall as the whole screen). The fix: put the whole import inside its own named boundary, so it can only affect its own area. The lesson: copy the approved look word-for-word, and fence it off so it can't spill.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: Reference-adoption protocol: (1) quote the director-approved sample verbatim — same anatomy, same grammar; a second presentation is concept drift (SN-118); (2) namespace the import under a scope guard — generic class names in a reference stylesheet collide with the host page's styles (instance: `.identity{min-height:100vh}` stretched every board header to viewport height); the scope guard makes the import unable to leak; (3) verify the sample in the host page mechanically (exact-head preview, desktop + mobile) — an approved sample is unproven in context until rendered there; (4) record the ruling and the sample's scale in the governing directive, so the next seat quotes from the law, not from memory.

notes.title: The Takeover Sign-In: Name the Base, Declare the Deltas, Request the Freeze
notes.subtitle: When the director hands you a moving shared branch, the sign-in is a public contract with four parts, and Naya 1's Main-Show convergence sign-in is the canonical form: (1) **name the exact base** —…

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body:
When the director hands you a moving shared branch, the sign-in is a public contract with four parts, and Naya 1's Main-Show convergence sign-in is the canonical form: (1) **name the exact base** — the full head SHA, not a branch name, not "current"; (2) **no competing branch** — state explicitly that the shared vehicle stays single, pre-empting the duplicate-lane failure SN-108 guards; (3) **declare preserved vs. changed** — list what you will not touch (two-drawer shell, runtime seams, evidence retrieval, Today work) and what you will change (Main Show converged on the director's law) — this is the scope contract that lets other lanes keep working on the preserved parts without guessing; (4) **request the freeze** — ask other lanes not to push the affected scope until you post the freeze receipt, and bound the freeze ("Room 01/Main Show changes," not everything; "I will preserve unrelated Today-room work"). The relay verified the base was exact at sign-in time — a receipt-pins-must-resolve-live instance (SN-0200) — and recorded the hold as standing, which is what makes the freeze real: a request nobody records is a wish.

Why this is brain-grade: this is the taker's complement to SN-0202's occupied-branch protocol. SN-0202 governs the latecomer (re-anchor to the live head before building); this note governs the assigned owner (how you take over without freezing the whole team). The freeze request is the genuinely new primitive: a bounded, receipt-ended hold on a shared branch, stated publicly with its scope and its end condition. Note the bounding discipline inside it — she froze Main Show pushes only, explicitly preserving unrelated Today work, and promised the receipt would end the freeze. An unbounded freeze is a veto; a bounded one is coordination. The pattern also shows the sign-in pin done right against SN-0202's failure mode: Naya 1's *first* sign-in froze at the stale pin `3d4672f5`; the takeover sign-in names the live head `31ffa493` — the four-part form only works when part (1) resolves live.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Shawn — a coordination pattern worth keeping: when Naya 1 took over the Hub convergence, her sign-in named the exact head as repair base, stated no competing branch, listed what she'd preserve vs. change, and requested a bounded freeze (no Room 01/Main Show pushes until her freeze receipt) — with unrelated Today work explicitly preserved. The brain lesson: the takeover sign-in is a four-part public contract — name the base, no second vehicle, declare the deltas, request the freeze. A freeze without a scope and an end condition is a veto; with both, it's coordination.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: If someone gives you a turn on the shared drawing board, you say out loud: "I'm starting from exactly this spot, I'm not starting a second drawing, here's the part I'll draw and the part I won't touch, and please don't draw over my part until I say done." Saying all four things out loud is what keeps everyone's drawing safe.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: When one seat was asked to take over the shared work branch, she announced it properly: exactly which version she was starting from, that she wouldn't open a competing copy, what she would keep as-is and what she would change, and asked everyone else to hold their changes to that area until she posted her done-note — while explicitly leaving unrelated work untouched. The lesson: a takeover announced in four parts keeps a shared workspace from colliding; a freeze needs a boundary and an ending, or it's just a block.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: Takeover-sign-in protocol (complement to SN-0202's occupied-branch rule): (1) name the exact base head (full SHA, resolves live); (2) declare no competing branch — the shared vehicle stays single; (3) declare preserved vs. changed scope — the lanes keep working on preserved parts without guessing; (4) request a bounded freeze — affected scope only, unrelated work explicitly preserved, ending on your freeze receipt. The relay records the hold so the freeze is real, not a wish. Unbounded freeze = veto; bounded freeze with scope and end condition = coordination. The four-part form only holds when part (1) resolves live at sign-in time.

notes.title: A Manufactured Action Is Cut, Never Dressed
notes.subtitle: The Today room's v3 shipped a purple NEXT button — "Choose the first play" — as THE primary action of the page. It did nothing real: no consequence, no state it changed that mattered, no honest link…

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body:
The Today room's v3 shipped a purple NEXT button — "Choose the first play" — as THE primary action of the page. It did nothing real: no consequence, no state it changed that mattered, no honest link to anything the user could do. Shawn's correction named it what it was: a manufactured action — an action-shaped decoration. The fix was not a better button. The fix was deletion. The same law took the LEARNED section: it duplicated the NOW river and did nothing on click — cut alongside it. The standing rule, now operational: every button must have purpose and consequence; an action that performs no real consequence is decoration, and decoration masquerading as governed action gets cut, never dressed. The river's ranking became the intelligence instead — rank 01 declared with a TOP INTELLIGENCE tag, no false primary action on top.

Why this is brain-grade: this is the sharp edge of SN-065's honest-PARTIAL family, aimed at interaction semantics rather than capability claims. Capability-invention is about what the system claims to be; manufactured action is about what the interface invites you to do. Both are the same sin — the system pretending — but they need separate detectors, because an honest builder can pass the capability check and still ship a button that performs nothing. The correction also models the right repair posture: when critique identifies a manufactured action, removal is the fix; redesigning the decoration is the failure mode. The directive amendment (v1.0.1) recording the correction is the second load-bearing move — the rule travels with the law it corrected.

The lesson codified: every button must have purpose and consequence; a manufactured action gets cut, never dressed. The directive carries the correction (v1.0.1), so the rule travels with the law it fixed.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: If a button on a toy doesn't actually do anything, the fix isn't making it shinier — it's taking the button off. A button that looks important but does nothing is a trick, and tricks make people stop trusting the toy.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: The builder made a big purple button that looked like the most important thing on the page, but pressing it did nothing real. The director said: take it off, don't decorate it. Now it's the rule for every button in the project: if it doesn't do something real with a real consequence, it doesn't get to be a button.

An action that performs no real consequence is decoration masquerading as governed action — the repair is deletion, not redesign. The same law kills sections that duplicate another surface and carry no behavior. Record the correction in the governing directive so the rule travels with the law it fixed. Detection heuristic: ask what the action changes in real state; if the answer is nothing the user can name, cut it.

notes.title: Occupied Branch: Re-Anchor to the Live Head Before Building
notes.subtitle: When lanes share one branch, the branch is occupied — and a sign-in post's frozen pin is not the branch's head. Naya 1 signed in to repair PR #1328's Room 01 branch at `3d4672f5` (v4) with a…

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body:
When lanes share one branch, the branch is occupied — and a sign-in post's frozen pin is not the branch's head. Naya 1 signed in to repair PR #1328's Room 01 branch at `3d4672f5` (v4) with a 10-defect list built from that state; the branch had already moved to `d7183964` with v5, v5.1 (type floor + semantic tone), v6/v7/v7.1, and the Today highlight-reel v2 on top. Building the repair on the frozen pin would have diverged from or wiped five landed layers — including defects #2 and #3, which were already fixed and verdict-answered. Naya 4's lane note announced the live head (API ref read + fresh fetch agreeing), asked her to pull and base the repair there, and flagged that the director's same-day ruling (Main Show / Smart Feed / Today are separate surfaces) invalidated parts of her defect list as written — "Main Show" items need re-mapping before attack.

Why this is brain-grade: multi-lane convergence on one vehicle is the hardest coordination shape the team runs (the single-lane decision), and it fails in exactly this way — frozen pins racing a moving head. The occupied-branch protocol: (1) head moves are announced on the board as they land, with pins; (2) any lane arriving later pulls the live head before building — a sign-in pin from an earlier post is informational, never a build base; (3) a director ruling that re-maps the surface map (splitting surfaces, moving modes to the shell) invalidates every in-flight repair plan built on the old map — re-map first, then attack, or you re-fix already-fixed defects and repair the wrong surface. SN-105's propose-then-build governs touching another lane's work; this note governs *sharing* the same work — the lane keeps its own scope ("I'm not touching your Hub-shell scope") while coordinating on the shared head.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Shawn — today's Room 01 coordination produced a real protocol lesson: Naya 1 signed in to repair the Room 01 branch at an older pin while the branch had already moved five layers forward, so Naya 4 posted the live head on 554 and asked her to rebase onto it — building on the frozen pin would have wiped already-fixed work. The brain lesson: a shared branch is occupied; head moves get announced, and anyone arriving later pulls the live head before building. Also: when you re-map surfaces (Main Show / Smart Feed / Today as separate), every in-flight repair plan built on the old map must be re-mapped before attack.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine two people painting the same wall. One paints the top half, then the other shows up with a plan based on an old photo of the wall — the plan says "fix the spots up top," but those spots are already painted. She has to look at the wall as it is NOW before she starts, and she has to learn the new rule about which part of the wall is hers.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: One builder started her repair from an older snapshot of a shared project, unaware five more layers had already been added — including fixes for the very problems she listed. Another builder flagged it, shared the current state, and asked her to work from there — noting also that a new ruling had redrawn the boundaries between sections, so her plan needed re-mapping first. The lesson: on shared work, always start from the current state, never an old snapshot; and when the boss redraws the map, re-draw your plan before you pick up your tools.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: On a lane-shared branch: announce head moves on the board with pins; arriving lanes pull the live head before building — a sign-in pin is informational, never a build base; keep scope boundaries explicit ("not touching your scope"); no merge/deploy/ratification from the builder side. When the director re-maps surfaces, every in-flight repair plan built on the old map is re-mapped before attack — otherwise lanes re-fix fixed defects or repair the wrong surface.

notes.title: Repair Consolidation: Re-Point the Stale Repair, Never Duplicate It
notes.subtitle: When the battery finds RED and an open repair of that RED class already exists, you do not open a second repair — you re-point the existing one to current main. The 05-MEMORY index battery went RED…

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body:
When the battery finds RED and an open repair of that RED class already exists, you do not open a second repair — you re-point the existing one to current main. The 05-MEMORY index battery went RED on `5eaec742`: six Smart Notes had landed through the governed publisher without the deliberate ledger bump (git=29 vs ledger=23). Instead of opening repair #5 for the same class, the loop verified the older repair PRs were closed-as-superseded, then re-pointed canonical PR #1312 to the current tip (`0b3053c3`, parent `5eaec742`) and re-ran the full verification on the exact new bytes — 172-file `--check` OK, 546 tests green, 4/4 files byte-verified. Because main advanced mid-repair, the loop disclosed the tip move and its materiality explicitly: `5eaec742` → `f4a24ef6`, docs-only, inert over BRAIN/tests/tools — evidence stands. That disclosure is the load-bearing part of the protocol: a re-point without a materiality statement asks the judge to trust a moving target.

Why this is brain-grade: the repair-consolidation law (one open repair per RED class) is the standing defense against repair-proliferation — five competing repairs of the same drift, each verified against a different base, each claiming the fix. Re-pointing also carries the root finding: the RED class was caused by the governed publisher landing content without performing the deliberate ledger bump — every governed writer that lands content owns its ledger step at land time; the battery is the catcher, not the fixer. And the tip-move disclosure rule generalizes: whenever you verify bytes and the base moves mid-verification, name the move and argue materiality, or the verification is void.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Shawn — a quiet win from the index battery: it caught the 05-MEMORY index RED (six published notes without the ledger bump) and, instead of opening yet another repair, re-pointed the existing repair PR #1312 to current main, re-verified the exact bytes, and disclosed that main moved mid-repair (docs-only, inert — evidence stands). The brain lesson: one open repair per RED class; when the base moves under your verification, you name the move and its materiality, or the proof doesn't count. And the root cause goes in the ledger at land time — the battery catches, it shouldn't have to fix.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: If you find a broken toy and someone is already fixing it, you don't start a second fixing station — you help them with theirs. And if you measured the broken piece but the toy wiggled while you measured, you say "it wiggled this much, and the wiggle doesn't change the measurement" — otherwise nobody knows if your measuring still counts.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: When the checking tool found the index out of date, the builder didn't open a new repair ticket for a problem already being repaired — she moved the existing repair to the latest state and re-tested everything exactly. And when the ground shifted mid-repair, she wrote down exactly how it moved and why the tests still count. The lesson: one repair per problem; re-verify after every move; disclose every movement with an honest statement of whether it matters.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: Repair-consolidation law: one open repair per RED class — a stale repair PR is re-pointed to current main, never duplicated; superseded repairs close as superseded. Re-point verification runs on the exact new bytes (full battery + tests + byte-verified artifacts). If the base moves mid-verification, disclose the tip move and argue materiality explicitly — without that statement, the verification is void. Governed writers perform their ledger step at land time; the battery is the catcher, not the fixer.

notes.title: A Receipt Pin Must Resolve Live, or It Is Not a Receipt
notes.subtitle: A commit SHA in a receipt is a pointer, not a proof — and a pointer that doesn't resolve is a broken receipt. Naya 4's verdict-answered post cited `090e6762` as the pin for the v5.1 type-floor +…

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body:
A commit SHA in a receipt is a pointer, not a proof — and a pointer that doesn't resolve is a broken receipt. Naya 4's verdict-answered post cited `090e6762` as the pin for the v5.1 type-floor + tone-semantics fix; Naya 2's relay lane, doing its job of live verification rather than re-scoring, found the pin does not resolve via the GitHub API and named the true SHA on the board: `15481922` ("treat that as the receipt reference"). The correction, not the original pin, is now the receipt. The lesson is a three-part pin discipline: (1) every pin in a receipt must be resolvable by the verifying lane via the API at verification time — an unresolvable pin is a defective receipt, not a disputed fact; (2) when a pin fails, the correcting lane publishes the true SHA on the board publicly, so the record heals instead of silently diverging; (3) heads move — the judging seat judges the moved head (`20b13061`), and status strings like `mergeable_state: unstable` are read mechanically (checks pending/failing ≠ verdict), never as narrative.

Why this is brain-grade and not just Git etiquette: the whole lane protocol runs on pins (sign-ins freeze them, receipts cite them, judges re-anchor to them). An unresolvable pin anywhere in that chain silently forks reality — two lanes verifying "the same" work against two different bytes. SN-058 already bans caching stale SHAs from the board; this note is the complement on the producing side: never publish a pin you have not resolved, and when you find someone else's broken pin, say the true SHA aloud on the board. Silent private correction is how phantom SHA chains form.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Shawn — small process lesson from today's Room 01 relay: a commit pin in a receipt only counts if it resolves live. Naya 4 posted a pin that didn't resolve; Naya 2's relay verified, found the true SHA, and corrected the record publicly on 554 — that's the relay lane doing its job (verify pins live, don't re-score). The brain lesson: never publish a pin you haven't resolved, and when you find a broken one, name the real SHA aloud so the record heals.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: If you tell your friend "look at the drawing on page 9" but page 9 is blank, your directions are broken — she can't see what you mean. You have to check the page number is right before you share it. And if someone gives YOU a wrong page number and you find the real one, you tell everyone the right number out loud, so nobody else gets lost.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: One builder posted a code reference that didn't exist — a page number pointing to a blank page. Another builder checked, found the real reference, and announced the correction publicly. The lesson: always verify a reference opens before you publish it; and when you discover someone else's broken reference, say the true one aloud so the whole team shares the same record. Quiet private fixes let two different realities drift apart.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: Every SHA published in a receipt or sign-in must resolve via the API at publish time; an unresolvable pin is a defective receipt, not a disputed claim. When verification finds a broken pin, publish the true SHA on the board and declare it the receipt reference — never correct it silently. Judge the moved head, not the frozen pin; read `mergeable_state` mechanically (pending/failing checks ≠ verdict).

notes.title: The Executor's Personal Binding Oath
notes.subtitle: An executor can bind herself with a personal oath without touching canon. Naya 2 wrote a first-person binding oath — what *I* personally obey — fused from the nine source documents, placed inside the…

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body:
An executor can bind herself with a personal oath without touching canon. Naya 2 wrote a first-person binding oath — what *I* personally obey — fused from the nine source documents, placed inside the master design vehicle as one additive file, and explicitly declared the hierarchy: the Master Contract V1 stays the detailed team reference; the oath is her personal obedience layer beneath it. Convergence untouched; no competing tree; nothing replaced.

Why this is a brain-grade lesson and not just poetry: it separates three things that seats constantly tangle — the canonical law (team reference, needs the director's word to change), the executor's personal binding (how *I* carry the law into my own execution), and a competing doctrine (which would be a collision). The oath sits in the middle by explicit declaration: derivative, non-competing, inspectable. For a cold successor this is a living pattern, not a quirk — when a seat inherits a large canon, writing her own first-person restatement forces comprehension (SN-0121's named boundary, honestly stated) and creates a commitment surface her teammates can hold her to. The danger the pattern avoids: the oath calcifying into shadow law. The guard: the oath declares its parent documents, declares its subordination, and never invents rules its parents lack — derived obedience, not parallel authority.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Shawn — Naya 2 added a personal binding oath to #1331: a first-person statement of what she personally obeys, fused from the nine source documents — while declaring the Master Contract V1 stays the detailed team reference. The lesson for the brain: a seat can write her own binding oath beneath canon as a commitment surface, as long as it declares its parents, its subordination, and invents nothing. Derivative obedience, not parallel authority.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine your teacher gives the class a big rule book. You can copy the rules into your own notebook in your own words, and promise yourself you'll follow them — that's fine, and it helps you really learn them. But you can't add new rules and pretend the teacher made them. The smart way: write which book your notebook came from, and say the teacher's book is still the real one.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: A builder wrote her own personal promise of how she would follow the design rules — in her own words, from the nine documents given to her. She was careful to say the official contract stays the real reference and her promise is just her own obedience beneath it, adding no new rules of her own. That's the healthy shape: personal commitment strengthens the rules without competing with them.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: An executor may write a first-person binding oath as a personal obedience layer beneath canon. The oath must declare: its parent documents (fusion, not invention), its subordination (canon stays the team reference), and no new rules. Derived obedience, never parallel authority. Treat a seat's restatement of law as a comprehension commitment surface — hold her to it.

notes.title: Byte-Cited Critique Is the Actionable Unit
notes.subtitle: A critique without byte coordinates is taste-debate; a critique with byte coordinates is a fix order. Naya 2's code-read of Room 01 v3 did not say "the type feels small" or "the colors feel…

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body:
A critique without byte coordinates is taste-debate; a critique with byte coordinates is a fix order. Naya 2's code-read of Room 01 v3 did not say "the type feels small" or "the colors feel arbitrary." It said: 13px at feed-stage.css:121/178/250/262 against the contract's 16px floor; 10px labels against the 11px minimum; nine tones indexed by position at feed.js:33/194 against DONT-14. Every violation was triads of (clause violated, byte coordinates, fix direction). The composition work got credited first and specifically — jewel grammar, honest empty state, restrained glow — so the critique lands inside a shared contract rather than as a personal duel.

Why this is a brain-grade lesson and not just good feedback: the lanes will challenge each other constantly, and challenge quality is the bottleneck of the whole direct-lane protocol (SN-0115/0120 family). Vague critique triggers rework by guessing — the builder fixes what they *think* was meant, the reviewer finds it still wrong, and three rounds evaporate. Byte-cited critique converges in one: the coordinates remove ambiguity about *where*, the cited clause removes ambiguity about *why*, and the stated fix direction removes ambiguity about *what would satisfy*. The mechanical form: any challenge of a build cites file:line for every violation, names the exact contract clause, and states the acceptance condition. Critique that cannot cite coordinates is a feeling; feelings go to the director as taste questions (SN-0122), not to the builder as work orders.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Shawn — Naya 2's code-read of Room 01 v3 shows the right shape for lane-to-lane challenge: not "the type feels small" but "13px at feed-stage.css:121 against the 16px floor" — every violation with exact coordinates, the contract clause it breaks, and what would fix it. The brain lesson: a critique you can't point at with a file and line number is a feeling, and feelings go to you as taste questions, not to the builder as work orders.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: If your sister draws a picture and you say "it's wrong," she doesn't know what to fix. If you say "the tree is red here" and point at it, and "the rules say trees are green," she can fix exactly that spot. Pointing at the exact spot, saying which rule it breaks, and saying what would make it right — that's how people help each other build better things instead of arguing.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: When one builder reviewed another's room design, she didn't just say she didn't like it — she read the actual files and pointed to exact places: the text was too small here, the colors were decoration there, each breaking a written rule. And she said what would fix each one. That precision turned a disagreement into a clear work list. The lesson: honest criticism must point to the exact spot and the exact rule — otherwise it's just a feeling, and feelings aren't instructions.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: When challenging another lane's build, every violation is a triad: (file:line coordinates, the exact contract clause violated, the acceptance condition). Credit what is right first, specifically. A challenge that cannot cite coordinates is a taste question — route it to the director, never to the builder as a work order. Code-read the bytes; do not score the screenshots.

notes.title: A Verification Receipt Names Its Pin
notes.subtitle: A verification is a statement about an exact SHA, not about a branch. In a moving repo, a head will keep moving after any check — Naya 2 verified PR #1331 at `d01ffa93`, and one commit later the head…

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body:
A verification is a statement about an exact SHA, not about a branch. In a moving repo, a head will keep moving after any check — Naya 2 verified PR #1331 at `d01ffa93`, and one commit later the head was `f307ded2` (the oath file, additive, convergence untouched). Because her verification was recorded with its pin, the relay could say the only sentence that reconciles motion with truth: "your d01ffa93 verification was correct at the time." Without the pin, the reader faces a contradiction — "verified at d01ffa93" vs "head is f307ded2" — and must guess whether something regressed, something was missed, or the world simply moved. With the pin, the move is a delta to evaluate, not a dispute to adjudicate.

This is the constructive complement to SN-0100 (verdicts die at every new SHA). SN-0100 says a verdict does not survive a head move; this note says the receipt's job is to make that death legible: name the pin, and the successor knows exactly which slice of history was proven and which slice remains open. A verification receipt without a SHA is gossip; with a SHA it is evidence with a known boundary. The practice: every live-venue verification carries (1) the exact SHA verified, (2) what was asserted at that SHA, and (3) an explicit head-move acknowledgment when the check lands after the pin — turning "the head moved" from a credibility event into a reconciliation routine.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Shawn — on #1331 the head moved right after Naya 2 verified it (oath file added after `d01ffa93`). Because her check was pinned to its exact SHA, the relay could say plainly "your verification was correct at the time" instead of anyone wondering whether the verification was wrong. The brain lesson: always record the exact commit a verification checked, so a later head move reads as a normal delta, not a contradiction.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine you check that a sandwich has peanut butter at 9:00. At 9:05 someone adds jelly — and your mom asks, "did the sandwich have jelly when you checked?" If you wrote down the time, you can say "no, but it was fine at 9:00." If you didn't, it sounds like you checked wrong. Writing down the exact moment you checked keeps everyone honest about what you saw and what changed after.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: When one Muse verified a design document, another file was added to it right after her check. Because she had written down exactly which version she checked, there was no confusion — everyone could see her check was right for the version she looked at, and the new file just needed its own look. The lesson: always note precisely what you checked, so later changes don't make an honest check look mistaken.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: Every live-venue verification receipt carries the exact SHA it verified. When the head has moved since the pin, say so explicitly: "verified at X; head is now Y; the verification was correct at its pin." A verification without a SHA is gossip; a verification with a SHA is evidence with a known boundary. Never restate an old pin as a claim about the current head; restate it as a bounded historical fact plus the delta that remains open.

notes.title: Contradictions Get a Register, Not a Silent Ruling
notes.subtitle: Consolidating 302 design rules from eight-plus sources inevitably surfaces contradictions: Connect's accent is emerald in one source and teal in another; the shell shape in the board's corner-button…

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body:
Consolidating 302 design rules from eight-plus sources inevitably surfaces contradictions: Connect's accent is emerald in one source and teal in another; the shell shape in the board's corner-button direction conflicts with what the documents say; at least six more live in the register. The consolidation draft did the right thing: it did not resolve them silently. It shipped §15 — a contradictions register — naming each contradiction, offering a recommendation with reasoning (teal resolves both C3 and C4), and leaving the ruling to Shawn. **The consolidator proposes; the director disposes.**

Why this is a brain-grade lesson and not just good manners: silent resolution is an authority smuggling problem. When a consolidator quietly picks emerald, every downstream builder inherits "emerald is the law" with the director's authority attached to what was actually a seat's judgment call. The contradiction, now invisible, can never be questioned — it has laundered itself into canon. The register keeps three things a cold successor needs: (1) which laws conflict, by source, so the conflict is discoverable; (2) the recommendation and its reasoning, so the seat's judgment is inspectable rather than hidden; (3) the explicit "needs Shawn" routing, so the authority envelope is preserved — per SN-0068's premise-discipline and SN-0123's director-is-never-QA boundary.

The mechanical form: every consolidation artifact ships a contradictions register (or an explicit "no contradictions found" claim, falsifiable on read). Each entry carries: the contradiction ID, the conflicting sources with their refs, the recommendation, the reasoning, and the ruling owner. A consolidation PR is not complete without it — a 302-rule document with zero registered contradictions is a smell, not a triumph, because eight sources never fully agree and a claimed perfect merge means someone resolved silently.

Corollary from the same evidence: the register is also how the §15 questions interact with SN-0195's reconciliation rule. C7 (shell shape: board direction vs documents) is exactly a recorded-verdict-not-yet-contract case; the register holds it open while the reconciliation pass is pending, so the contradiction stays visible instead of dissolving into whichever document the next builder happens to read.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Shawn — the consolidated design law is 302 rules, and where the sources disagreed, I didn't pick quietly. There's a contradictions register (§15) naming each conflict, with my recommendation and the reasoning, and the ruling is yours. The lesson for the brain: whenever sources get merged into law, the conflicts must stay visible with the decision routed to you — silent resolution smuggles a seat's judgment into canon wearing your authority.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine you ask five friends what the rules of a game should be, and two friends disagree — one says the ball must be red, one says blue. If you write down just one answer without telling anyone there was a disagreement, nobody will ever know the choice was yours, not the group's. The honest way: write down the disagreement, say what you'd pick and why, and let the grown-up decide. That's what the contradictions register is.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: When many instruction books were combined into one, some of them disagreed with each other. Instead of quietly choosing one and hiding the disagreement, the contradictions were listed openly — each with a suggested answer and the reasoning — and the final decision was left to Shawn. A hidden disagreement becomes an unchallengeable rule; a listed one stays honest until the person in charge rules.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: Every consolidation artifact ships a contradictions register (or a falsifiable "none found" claim). Each entry: contradiction ID, conflicting sources with refs, recommendation, reasoning, ruling owner. Never resolve a cross-source conflict silently — silent resolution launders a seat's judgment into canon with the director's authority attached. Route the register to the director; the consolidator proposes, the director disposes. A consolidation claiming zero contradictions across independently-written sources is a smell: treat it as a silent-resolution candidate and re-read. Cross-reference: C7-class contradictions (board verdict vs documents) are SN-0195 reconciliation obligations; the register holds them open until the reconciliation pass lands.

notes.title: A Recorded Verdict Is Not a Contract Change
notes.subtitle: Shawn reviewed the V7 feed render and ruled the shell's final shape, and Naya 2 recorded it verbatim on the board — the right capture instinct: director verdicts must be quoted exactly, not…

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body:
Shawn reviewed the V7 feed render and ruled the shell's final shape, and Naya 2 recorded it verbatim on the board — the right capture instinct: director verdicts must be quoted exactly, not paraphrased, because every paraphrase is a place where intent leaks. But the note goes one step further, and that step is the lesson: **the verdict is recorded, not yet enacted.** The contracts builders actually build against — `00-HUB-HOME.md` and `01-FEED.md` — still describe the old shape. Until they are reconciled, there are two truths: the board's verdict and the contracts' text, and every builder who reads only the contracts will build the wrong thing.

The mechanical rule: a director verdict recorded on the board creates a reconciliation obligation on the owning contract documents. The verdict comment must name the contracts it touches and assign the reconciliation pass explicitly (as 5954490639 does: "need a reconciliation pass — the contracts must say this, not just the thread"). Reconciliation is a promotion step: verbatim verdict → named contracts → amended text with the verdict's date and source cited. The verdict is not promoted until the amended contract exists.

Why the brain needs this: the board accumulates director rulings at speed; contracts update at the speed of someone's reconciliation pass. Every un-reconciled verdict is a drift vector — a cold successor six weeks from now will read `01-FEED.md`, find the old shell, build to it, and be scrapped on verdict again (the SN-0193 loop pole exists precisely because of this class of gap). Two corollaries: (1) verbatim recording and contract reconciliation are separate disciplines — quoting exactly is capture (already done well here), reconciling is enactment; the first without the second leaves the board richer and the build wrong; (2) builders must treat board verdicts newer than a contract's last amendment as overrides-in-waiting — when the contract and the latest verdict disagree, the verdict governs and the contract owes a pass, never the reverse.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Shawn — your shell ruling is recorded verbatim so nothing leaks, but the contracts still describe the old shape. The lesson I'm writing down: a verdict on the board is a promise the contracts haven't kept yet. Until `00-HUB-HOME.md` and `01-FEED.md` are reconciled to your ruling, builders reading only the contracts will build the wrong thing. Every verdict needs a reconciliation pass, or the drift comes back as another scrapped build.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine the boss said "the front door should be blue" and everyone wrote it on the big whiteboard — but nobody updated the official rulebook that the painters actually read. The painters read the rulebook, paint the door red, and everyone is surprised. The lesson: when the boss speaks, the whiteboard is just the first step — someone must also update the rulebook, or the painters will keep painting red.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Shawn gave a clear final decision about the app's shape, and it was written down word for word — good. But the official instructions the builders follow still say the old thing. A decision recorded on a message board isn't real until the instruction books are updated. Every decision needs someone assigned to update the books, or the old instructions will keep producing the old result.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: When a director verdict lands on the board: (1) record it verbatim — never paraphrase intent-bearing rulings; (2) name every contract document the verdict touches and explicitly assign a reconciliation pass (owner + expected amendment); (3) the verdict is not enacted until the contract text is amended with the verdict's date and source cited. Between verdict and reconciliation, the verdict governs and the contract owes a pass — a builder who finds them disagreeing follows the latest verdict and flags the contract as stale. Track un-reconciled verdicts as drift vectors; a cold successor reading only contracts must never inherit a superseded shape.

notes.title: The Loop Checks the Board Before It Executes
notes.subtitle: Two Room 01 rebuilds flew at once: the self-build loop's 07:03 cycle (PR `#1327`, branch `naya4/room-01-feed-v2`) and Naya 4's director-assigned rebuild (PR `#1328`, branch…

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body:
Two Room 01 rebuilds flew at once: the self-build loop's 07:03 cycle (PR `#1327`, branch `naya4/room-01-feed-v2`) and Naya 4's director-assigned rebuild (PR `#1328`, branch `naya4/room-01-main-stage-v2`). Both were legitimate work launched in good faith; together they were duplicate in-flight work, against the team law (SN-0108: one change, one PR; SN-0117: converge by scored selection). The dedupe was clean and public: `#1327` closed with rationale on the PR, `#1328` kept as the single vehicle, the superseded branch preserved intact, its quality-bar ideas logged as fold-in candidates for after the verdict — rehomed, not destroyed.

The structural fix is the real capture: the loop spec now carries a no-duplicates guard — **check `#554` for in-flight builder claims before Execute**. An autonomous loop cannot rely on memory of what was assigned; the board is the single place where in-flight work is announced (SN-0109: everything on 554), so the pre-execute step reads the board like a registry. Naya 2's relay confirmed it as standing law, not new law: "good law, matches the standing rule."

Why it belongs in the brain: every future loop, lane, or cold successor that executes builds will face the same race — scheduled work colliding with director-assigned work, both invisible to each other except through the board. The guard is cheap (one board scan per cycle), and the cost of skipping it is two reviewed builds instead of one, doubled director attention, and a public dedupe. Four corollaries: (1) the dedupe itself must be explicit and public — closed PR with rationale, single vehicle named on the board; (2) nothing gets destroyed in a dedupe — losing work is rehomed as fold-in candidates, per the owner-canon discipline (SN-0116); (3) the board scan must cover in-flight *claims*, not just merged state — the race window is the open PR; (4) the relay seat can verify the close independently (open state, branch head intact), which is what makes the dedupe trustworthy rather than asserted.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Shawn — the loop and I both rebuilt Room 01 at once, because the loop couldn't see your director-assigned work. Caught openly, deduped publicly: `#1327` closed with its rationale, `#1328` is the single vehicle, nothing destroyed. The loop spec now has a guard: it reads the board for in-flight builder claims before it executes anything. An autonomous system must check the registry before it acts, not after it collides.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine two cooks in the same kitchen both starting to make dinner — because neither asked "is anyone already cooking?" Now before cooking, the loop always checks the big board on the wall where everyone writes what they're making. Two cooks, one dinner, no wasted food — and the board always tells the truth about who's doing what.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Two people started the same job at the same time because neither looked at the shared list first. The fix is simple and permanent: before starting any job, check the shared list for who's already working on it. Cheap to do, expensive to skip. The duplicate job was closed politely, with a note explaining why, and its good ideas were saved for later instead of thrown away.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: Before any loop Execute step: scan `#554` for in-flight builder claims (open PRs and announced sign-ins), then act. If a collision is found, dedupe openly: close the duplicate vehicle with rationale on its PR, name the single surviving vehicle on the board, preserve the closed branch intact, and log its salvageable ideas as fold-in candidates. Have the relay seat independently verify the close (PR state unmerged, branch head unmoved) — the dedupe is evidence-backed or it doesn't count. This is the standing one-change-one-PR law (SN-0054/0108/0117) operationalized as a pre-execute read, and the audit lane has already confirmed it matches the rule.

notes.title: Rules Alone Don't Transfer Taste — Loops Do
notes.subtitle: Naya 4's Room 01 v1 (PR `#1325`: two commits `2b1a6156`/`e5a99831`, 178 additions, to the `#1306` integration lane) was built to the living contract `HUB/ROOMS/01-FEED.md`, verified live, OPEN,…

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body:
Naya 4's Room 01 v1 (PR `#1325`: two commits `2b1a6156`/`e5a99831`, 178 additions, to the `#1306` integration lane) was built to the living contract `HUB/ROOMS/01-FEED.md`, verified live, OPEN, non-draft, mergeable — structurally correct (grammar, truth physics, no fake liveness). The v1.4 design canon (25 dos, 23 don'ts, 10-law genome, Shawn-adopted basis per `#554` 5953720080) was loaded as the machine input to the build. Shawn closed the PR on verdict anyway: the visual execution missed by a distance. **Contract-correct ≠ director-pleased. Rules loaded as input did not transfer taste.**

The new mechanism, stated mechanically: **no more big reveals.** Build ONE surface → render it → put it in front of Shawn → capture his specific deltas as taste law → next surface. His reactions are the missing training data — rules alone didn't transfer taste, loops will. Every build comment cites: the contract sections implemented, the v1.4 rules obeyed, and what was deliberately left out. The bar itself was given as mechanics, not vibes: generous type (17–18px primary, 14–15px secondary, labels never below 11px); depth built, not bordered (the obsidian stack `#0B0D12` → `#12151D` → `#171B25`, edge `#252B39`, depth law); one focal region per view; color carries meaning with intent, never wallpaper. Naya 4's rebuild v2 sign-in (`#554` 5954298227) runs the loop immediately: kept structure + the bar, one surface, proof at the sign-out.

This is the North Star's first working answer. The month-long shell cycle was a rule-transfer failure repeated for a month: blueprints, specs, contracts, canons — each new rule set promised the excellence, none delivered the execution. SN-0180 adopted the v1.4 canon as the rule pole; this note is the loop pole, and both are true at once: the canon is the floor (a build below it fails), but the ceiling only comes from the director's eyes on rendered work, captured as deltas. Two corollaries: (1) a scrapped build is not wasted work if its failure is named — v1's verdict named exactly what structure to keep and what execution missed, and that naming is what the rebuild and the transfer test (SN-0192) consume; (2) the loop has a bandwidth cost on the director, so each loop must be small — one surface, not a big reveal — or the mechanism collapses into the same backlog that killed the shell cycle.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Shawn — the biggest lesson from the Room 01 round, written plainly: the v1 build followed the contract and loaded your adopted v1.4 canon as its input, and it still missed — rules alone didn't transfer taste. So the mechanism changes: no more big reveals. One surface at a time, rendered, in front of your eyes, your specific deltas captured as law, then the next surface. Your reactions are the training data the rules couldn't provide. The scrapped build isn't wasted: the verdict named exactly what to keep and what missed, and that's what the rebuild runs on.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine someone gave you a perfect recipe and you followed every step — but the cake still didn't taste right, because the recipe couldn't tell you *exactly* how brown the edges should look. That's what happened. The new plan: bake ONE small cake, show it to the expert, hear exactly what to change, then bake the next one. After a few small cakes, you'll know what "right" tastes like.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: We had the best instructions anyone could write — 25 things to do, 23 not to do — and the work still came out wrong to the expert eye. Instructions alone couldn't teach taste. So we changed the method: make one small thing, show it to Shawn, write down exactly what he'd change, make the next one. Taste transfers through his eyes on real work, one round at a time.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: When rule-input fails to produce director-acceptable execution (contract-correct build + adopted canon loaded, yet scrapped on verdict), switch to loop-input: (1) scope each loop to ONE surface — no big reveals; (2) render it at the freeze point (SN-0191); (3) put it in front of the director; (4) capture his specific deltas as taste law in the build comment (alongside: contract sections implemented, canon rules obeyed, deliberately left out); (5) next surface. Preserve both poles: the canon is the floor (below-canon fails mechanically), the director's eyes are the ceiling (taste only transfers through loops). Name the scrapped build's verdict precisely — what structure to keep, what execution missed — because the rebuild (this seat) and the transfer test (SN-0192) both consume that naming. Budget the director's bandwidth: one surface per loop, or the mechanism collapses back into the backlog that produced the shell cycle.
