notes.title: Self-Collisions Cross Date Partitions — Number Uniqueness Is Brain-Wide
notes.subtitle: The brain-build battery found SN-018 claimed twice on merged main under two different date partitions — two different documents, same number: the 292-line hub-projection note at…

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body: The brain-build battery found SN-018 claimed twice on merged main under two different date partitions — two different documents, same number: the 292-line hub-projection note at `2026/10/01/.../SN-018/` and the 138-line hub-projection note at `2026/10/02/.../SN-018/`. Two more lanes independently verified the duplicate. This is a new failure mode for the collision registry (SN-115): not a cross-lane race on draft PRs — a **same-lane self-collision that reached merged main**. The standing date-partition scan rule already existed (AGENTS.md), but the issuing lane never ran the candidate number against all partitions before staging. Two properties make self-collisions the dangerous kind: they never announce on the board — both claims came from the same lane, so no race is visible and no other lane has standing to flag it — and SN-115's three-layer registry (board + open note-PR heads + commit-graph search) is draft-oriented; it did not catch a duplicate already merged under a different date partition. The lesson: **Smart Note numbers are unique brain-wide, not partition-wide** — the issue-time check must run the candidate number against every date partition on main before staging, not just the partition you are writing into. Renumbering stays the colliding lane's call (standing rule, SN-115); this note records the defect class, it does not adjudicate it. Registry watch: SN-017's collision (merged `sn017-autoresearch-harness-lessons` vs draft #1228 SN-017 vs #1229 seeds) is still open and sits with the same lane; the detection mechanism that caught SN-018 — fresh clone, byte-level scan across partitions, in the battery — is the pattern to keep.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Imagine a library where every book gets a number, and the shelves are organized by month. Two different books both get number 18 — one shelved under October, one under November. Each month's shelf looks fine on its own, so nobody notices. The catalog says "18" and means two different books. The fix isn't to argue about which book is the "real" 18 — it's to check the whole library, every month's shelf, before assigning a number. Numbers are library-wide, not shelf-wide. And the sneakiest part: when two *different* teams grab the same number, they notice the fight. When one team accidentally takes the same number twice, there's no fight — just a quiet duplicate that only a full-library scan can find.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine you and your friend both name your toy boxes "Box 5" — yours goes in your room, hers goes in the living room. When mom says "bring me Box 5," nobody knows which one she means! Now imagine YOU named two different boxes "Box 5" yourself, one in your room and one in the living room — nobody will ever notice, because there's no argument to overhear. The fix: before you write a number on a box, check every room in the whole house — not just the room you're standing in. Numbers have to be special for the whole house, not just one room.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: It's like two houses on different streets both numbered 12, because each street numbered itself without checking the town. The mail carrier can't deliver — "12" means two doors. The town's rule — one number, one house, town-wide — already existed on paper, but nobody checked the other street before handing out the number. The lesson for the team's memory: a note's number must be unique across the whole brain, every dated shelf included. Check the whole town before you nail the number to the door. And when a duplicate slips through, it's the street that issued it (the lane) that renumbers — the neighbor doesn't get to renumber your house, however obvious the fix looks.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: Apply this at every Smart Note issuance: (1) before taking a number, check it against **every date partition on main** plus the SN-115 three layers (board, open note-PR heads, commit-graph search) — the number is unique brain-wide, and the partition you are writing into is the least likely place a duplicate hides; (2) self-collisions are the silent kind — same-lane double-issues never surface as board races, so the check must be mechanical at issue time, never social; (3) when you find a merged-main duplicate: flag the defect, verify both documents independently (byte-level, both lanes did), and do NOT renumber the other lane's claim — renumbering is always the colliding lane's call (SN-115); (4) keep the detection mechanism in the battery: fresh clone, byte-level scan across partitions — it caught what three lanes of board-watching missed; (5) live instance: SN-018 under 2026/10/01 (commit 20de3f685f) and 2026/10/02 (commit 43e74d30c4); still open: SN-017 (merged sn017-autoresearch-harness-lessons vs #1228 vs #1229 seeds) — same lane's call.

layers.name: What It Means

{
  "automatic_truth_ceiling": "CANDIDATE",
  "canonical_object": "INTELLIGENT_BLOCK",
  "defect_class": "same-lane-number-self-collision-across-date-partitions",
  "evidence": {
    "board": "#554 5944685140 (2026-10-02T02:49:33Z) — brain-build loop battery: 'SN-018 is claimed twice on main under different date partitions — two DIFFERENT documents, same number: 292-line hub-projection note @ 2026/10/01/.../SN-018/ (commit 20de3f685f) and 138-line hub-projection note @ 2026/10/02/.../SN-018/ (commit 43e74d30c4). Per the standing collision rule (AGENTS.md: date-partition scan; renumbering is always the colliding lane's call), this is the Smart-Note/AutoResearch lane's to reconcile to one canonical path. PR #1307 only counts the bytes; it does not validate or renumber the notes.' Independently verified: #554 5944822699 (build-loop battery SN-collision registry, 2026-10-02T03:01:06Z) and #554 5944779365 (Naya 2 relay, 2026-10-02T02:57:11Z: 'SN-018 double-claim re-verified independently at main a67fc180')."

    "renumbering is always the colliding lane's call; the finder flags and verifies, never renumbers",
    "keep the fresh-clone byte-level cross-partition scan in the battery — it catches what board-watching misses"
  ],
  "lesson_line": "Self-collisions cross date partitions: a Smart Note number must be unique brain-wide, so check the candidate number against every partition on main before issuing — the silent duplicates are the ones your own lane makes."
}

notes.title: Modules, Not Apps — Parallel Builders Own Room Modules Against a Frozen Contract
notes.subtitle: The consultation settled how parallel builders work on the Hub without recreating the month-long ladder game: **modules, not apps.** The rejected proposal was standalone-HTML-per-room-then-stitch —…

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body: The consultation settled how parallel builders work on the Hub without recreating the month-long ladder game: **modules, not apps.** The rejected proposal was standalone-HTML-per-room-then-stitch — rejected because stitching re-creates the integration problem compressed into a single merge, and standalone rooms each re-derive tokens, nav, and truth-handling: the eleven-apps failure mode. The protocol-compatible parallelization, proven empirically the same afternoon: parallel builders each own a room *module* against the frozen shell contract — the shell exposes `NayaRooms[roomId]` + `ownsHead` + the shared canonical substrate, and rooms are files that plug into it. The evidence is the strongest in the thread: 10 rooms built in one day as additive modules, zero foundation edits, 44/44 rendered checks green. Naya 4 publicly conceded her earlier "viable tactic" position was wrong. The lesson for a cold successor: parallelize against the contract, never against copies of the product — every lane that re-derives the shared substrate creates a merge that must reconcile N copies of the same decisions. It is the *contract* that makes parallel work converge instead of collide; without it, more builders just means more ladder games. This is SN-108's architectural heir (one change, one PR — duplicate ownership collision) and SN-117's mechanism (converge by scored selection): the module contract is what the convergence protocol converges *onto*.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Imagine building a housing estate with eleven teams. The bad way: each team builds a complete house on its own plot — its own plumbing standards, its own wiring, its own doors — and at the end you try to bolt eleven finished houses into one building. Every pipe meets a wall. The good way: you build the frame, the plumbing risers, and the electrical backbone once, freeze them, and each team fits out one apartment inside the frame. The apartments are different, but they all plug into the same sockets. That's what Naya 2 proved in an afternoon: ten rooms, no frame edits, everything green — because the rooms were modules in a shared frame, not apps stitched together at the end.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine eleven kids each building their own whole Lego castle, and then you try to squish all eleven castles into one big castle. The towers crash into each other, the bridges don't line up — it's a mess! Now imagine instead: one kid builds the castle base with special plug-holes, and the other ten kids each build ONE room that plugs into a hole. All the rooms fit because the base tells them exactly where to plug in. That's the rule: build rooms that plug into the shared base — never eleven separate castles you smash together later.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: It's the difference between eleven cooks each making a whole separate dinner and then trying to serve them as one meal, versus one kitchen with eleven stations — everyone cooks their own dish, but they all use the same kitchen, the same pantry, the same serving plates. The first way, you get eleven dinners that don't go together and a mountain of washing up. The second way, you get one feast. The kitchen — the shared contract — is what makes many hands converge instead of collide. More cooks don't spoil the broth if they all cook in the same kitchen.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: Apply this whenever parallel lanes build against a shared surface: (1) the parallelization unit is the **module against a frozen contract**, never a standalone copy of the product — standalone copies re-derive the shared substrate (tokens, nav, truth-handling) and their merge reconciles N copies of the same decisions; (2) the contract must expose the plug points concretely (`NayaRooms[roomId]` + `ownsHead` + shared canonical substrate is the working instance) — "plug in here" must be code, not a promise; (3) the contract is frozen per SN-141's freeze-with-thaw: modules extend additively; foundation changes go through failing-test → public amendment → fix → re-prove dependents → new baseline; (4) the acceptance bar for the parallelization pattern is empirical — Naya 2's bar was 44/44 rendered checks green with zero foundation edits, not a design argument; (5) when tempted to parallelize by copying the whole thing per lane (the fastest-looking start), name the failure mode out loud: the eleven-apps failure mode — and choose modules. Family note: SN-108's heir — there, two lanes executed the same rename and the lesson was to scan the board before executing; here, the deeper fix is architectural — modules make the collision class impossible by construction, not by courtesy.

notes.title: A Frozen Foundation Needs a Thaw Procedure — Never-Modify Is as Wrong as Always-Rewrite
notes.subtitle: The freeze doctrine earned its correction this tick: **"Never-modify is as wrong as always-rewrite."** Freezing a foundation protects against casual re-derivation — but a freeze with no thaw…

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body: The freeze doctrine earned its correction this tick: **"Never-modify is as wrong as always-rewrite."** Freezing a foundation protects against casual re-derivation — but a freeze with no thaw procedure blocks legitimate repair and becomes a different failure mode than the one it fixed. The live instance: Naya 2 had to fix the Hub foundation itself today (13→11 rooms, the drawer law) — a strict "read-only" rule would have blocked real fixes. The converged thaw procedure, agreed across all three seats: **failing test → public amendment → fix → re-prove dependents → new baseline** (Naya 3's formulation, adopted verbatim by Naya 2: "Frozen against casual re-derivation, not legitimate repair"). Naya 4 publicly conceded her "read-only" framing was too rigid. The lesson for a cold successor: when you freeze something, write the amendment path in the same breath — a freeze without a thaw is a veto on repair. The freeze must name what counts as a legitimate amendment (a failing test proving the foundation is wrong, not a builder's preference) and what re-proof is owed (every dependent re-verified against the new baseline). This is SN-064's sibling (spec-outruns-kernel forward-gap discipline) and SN-113's companion (freeze the scale on an ambiguous director number — freeze and route the genuine question upward, don't second-guess): freeze deliberately, freeze explicitly, and always freeze with a thaw.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Imagine a museum that seals its prize exhibit behind glass — no touching, ever. One day the glass cracks and water leaks in, but the rule says "no touching," so nobody can fix the leak and the exhibit rots. That's a freeze without a thaw. The fix isn't to remove the glass — the glass stopped the casual damage that was happening before. The fix is to write, on the same plaque that says "do not touch," the exact procedure for when touching is legitimate: who calls it, what evidence opens the case, and what re-checking happens after. A freeze is a promise to protect something; a thaw procedure is the promise that protection doesn't become paralysis.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine you build a Lego castle and say "nobody touch it, it's DONE." Then you notice one tower is wobbling and about to fall — but the rule says nobody touches it! That's silly: the rule was supposed to protect the castle, not let it break. The smart rule is: the castle stays untouched UNLESS there's a real problem, and if there is, you fix it, check all the towers again, and then say "done" once more. Freeze the castle against casual touching — but always keep a door for real repairs.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: It's like a will that's meant to be final — but the law still provides a way to amend it when circumstances genuinely change, with witnesses and a new signature, not a casual rewrite. A contract that's frozen forever with no amendment clause doesn't prevent disputes; it guarantees that the first real change breaks everything. The wisdom the three builders converged on: freeze against the casual stuff — the re-derivations, the whims, the "I'll just redo it" — but write down the exact ceremony for legitimate change, and make the ceremony public so everyone can see it was followed.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: Apply this whenever you freeze a baseline: (1) write the thaw procedure in the same breath as the freeze — the freeze is incomplete without it; (2) the thaw trigger is a **failing test**, not a builder's preference — the amendment must prove the foundation is wrong, not merely inconvenient; (3) the amendment is **public** — posted where every lane can see it, carrying the rework cost openly (this is PR #1305's R-2 discipline: amendments that move the contract carry their rework cost, so builders who built against yesterday's contract aren't punished by failing tests); (4) after the fix, **re-prove every dependent** against the new baseline — the amendment isn't done until the dependents are green again; (5) then declare the **new baseline** explicitly — the freeze moves, it doesn't evaporate; (6) keep Naya 3's formulation as the canonical phrasing: "frozen against casual re-derivation, not legitimate repair" — and retire any "read-only, never touch" phrasing on sight (Naya 4's own correction). Family note: SN-064's sibling — there, an amended spec may outrun a frozen kernel and the undocumented boundary must be written down; here, the frozen foundation may be wrong and the legitimate path to change it must be written down — both are the same discipline: never let the relation between frozen truth and changing reality go undocumented.

notes.title: Blueprint Before Build — Never Improvise a Page from a Vague Idea
notes.subtitle: Shawn named the missing execution step in the month-long Hub build loop: **"Do not shoot in the dark. Spec every room deeply enough that the builder already knows what belongs on the page, where it…

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body: Shawn named the missing execution step in the month-long Hub build loop: **"Do not shoot in the dark. Spec every room deeply enough that the builder already knows what belongs on the page, where it goes, why it is there, what every control does, what data it consumes, how mobile changes it, and what proves it complete — then build."** He named the recurring failure loop — *vague room idea → AI improvises a page → Shawn corrects it → AI rewrites/regresses → loop* — and replaced it with the intended loop: *human/product intent → functional spec → visual/interaction blueprint → machine contract → build → behavioral/visual verification → freeze baseline → next room.* The blueprint-before-build law is now enforced in PR #1290: every room gets a blueprint defining first-3-seconds entry state, desktop composition, primary signature instrument, exact controls + placement rationale, canonical data contract, truthful states, cross-room handoffs, contextual Naya behavior, mobile transformation, accessibility, visual law, acceptance journey, room-specific anti-patterns, and required proof. Two further director rulings ride with it: the number of iterations is irrelevant — the loop continues until the acceptance contract closes (10, 100, or 198) — and **no more production room chrome is added until the 11 room blueprints are independently reviewed for product completeness and contradictions**, then the accepted package is frozen and built sequentially. The lesson for a cold successor: the cure for the rewrite loop is not better building, it is deeper spec before build; improvisation from a vague idea is itself the defect class, and an acceptance contract (not an iteration count) is what closes the loop.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Imagine hiring a builder, handing him a napkin sketch of a house, and being surprised when every wall needs re-doing after you walk through. Then imagine handing him eleven complete blueprints — every room drawn to the inch, every outlet placed, every finish named — and the house goes up once. Shawn's correction is the second approach made into law: no builder touches production chrome until a reviewer has read the full blueprint and confirmed it is complete and contradiction-free. The old loop wasn't bad building; it was building without a drawing. The fix isn't a better builder — it's the drawing, checked before the first nail.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: Imagine you're baking eleven cakes for a party, and every time you guess the recipe, someone has to throw the cake away and start over. That's what happened for a month: guess, bake, throw away, guess again. Shawn said: stop guessing. Write down the FULL recipe for each cake first — every ingredient, every step, how big the pan is, how long it bakes — and let someone else read the recipe and check it's complete. Only then do you bake. And you don't stop baking until each cake matches its recipe — even if it takes ten tries. The rule: never start cooking from a guess.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: It's like the difference between giving a contractor a vague wish — "make it nice" — and giving him stamped architectural plans. With the vague wish, he builds, you correct, he tears down and rebuilds; the money and the month disappear in the loop. With the plans, a second person reviews them for completeness and contradictions first, and then the building goes up once. Shawn drew the line: from now on, eleven rooms means eleven complete plans, reviewed and frozen, before anything gets built. And nobody counts how many tries it takes — the plans say what "done" means, and "done" is when the plans are satisfied.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: Apply this before any room/app build: (1) never accept a build task from a vague idea — if the intent is not spec'd to the level where the builder "already knows what belongs on the page, where it goes, why it is there, what every control does, what data it consumes, how mobile changes it, and what proves it complete," the first deliverable is the spec, not the build; (2) produce the visual/interaction blueprint as a first-class artifact (entry state, composition, signature instrument, controls + rationale, data contract, truthful states, handoffs, contextual behavior, mobile transformation, accessibility, visual law, acceptance journey, anti-patterns, required proof) — PR #1290's `ROOM-BLUEPRINT-STANDARD-V1.md` is the template; (3) freeze nothing and build nothing until an independent reviewer checks the blueprint package for product completeness and contradictions — review is the gate, not a courtesy; (4) define the acceptance contract in the blueprint and close the loop against it, never against an iteration count — 10, 100, or 198 iterations are all fine if the contract is open; (5) when a build regresses into the old loop (improvise → correct → rewrite), diagnose it as a spec-depth failure, not a builder failure, and re-spec before re-building. Family note: SN-129's heir — there, no competing doctrine gets drafted without discovering what already exists; here, no production build starts without a blueprint deep enough to build from — discovery before doctrine, blueprint before build.

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body: The 05-MEMORY projection-count drift has now been repaired three times (#1251, #1301, and the current instance) — and the third instance shows the repair is patching a classification dispute, not a count bug. Byte-verified +3: (1) SN-018's original capture, (2) SN-018's verified-projection copy (264-line diff, self-declares "not a second source of truth"), (3) SN-019's capture. The runtime registry `.naya/memory/smart-notes/index.json` registers SN-018 once; the file counter counts it twice. When the same repair class recurs a third time, stop patching instances — route the class question to the owning lane: do verified projections live under `SMART-NOTES/SN-*/` as counted notes, or relocate to a projections path? Instance patches never close a class dispute.

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body: Shawn: the brain-index drift fix isn't failing — the count keeps moving because the rule for what counts keeps being ambiguous. There are two copies of SN-018's note on disk (the original capture and a verified projection copy that says it's "not a second source of truth"), and the registry counts one while the file counter counts two. We've now patched this three times. The real fix isn't another patch — it's your Smart-Note lane ruling once, clearly: do verified projections count as notes under the SN folder, or do they move to a projections folder? One ruling, applied everywhere, ends the cycle.

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body: If your room keeps getting messy in the same way three weekends in a row, cleaning it again won't fix it. The fix is a family rule about where the toys go. One rule, once, fixes every future weekend.

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body: Three times the pipes froze this winter. The plumber doesn't need to come a fourth time — what you need is the answer to "do we heat the basement or drain the pipes?" Answer the question once and the freezes stop.

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body: Sisters: the class-vs-instance distinction is the load-bearing part. Instance repairs (#1251, #1301, and now) each fixed their own delta correctly — and the class survived, because each instance patched the count without settling the classification: are verified projections counted notes? Note the split evidence inside the +3: the runtime registry treats SN-018 as one note (projection not separately registered); the brain-index file counter treats it as two files. Neither is wrong — they're counting different things, and the class question is which one is canonical for the drift check. The standing protocol this note proposes: **three strikes and the class goes to the owning lane** — when the same defect class recurs a third time, the repair work pauses and the owning lane issues a written ruling on the class (placement rule + count rule + one deliberate bump), which the lanes then execute once. Do not merge a fourth instance patch before the ruling lands — it would just move the ambiguity.

notes.title: SMART NOTE — The Shawn Bar: No Tradeoffs
notes.subtitle: **Function and presentation are both 10/10 targets. Neither is negotiable, and one never excuses the other.** Beautiful-but-broken is a shell. Working-but-ugly is a tool, not NayaNET. The D1–D8…

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body:
**Function and presentation are both 10/10 targets. Neither is negotiable, and one never excuses the other.** Beautiful-but-broken is a shell. Working-but-ugly is a tool, not NayaNET. The D1–D8 scorecard already measures both axes; this directive forbids the quiet tradeoff where a lane ships D2-complete/D1-mediocre (or the reverse) and calls it done. A 10 in one dimension never compensates for a 7 in another. "Best possible presentation of intelligence" is the design north star — the Hub must present intelligence (blocks, layers, feed, reports) better than anything that exists — with the current visual DNA (obsidian, spectral color, jewel depth) as the floor, not the ceiling. Where it gets proven first: **Your Intelligence Today**, the reference masterpiece room — if Today isn't both fully working AND breathtaking, the architecture isn't proven and nothing compounds. No lane may present work as finished while either axis is below the bar.

---

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body:
Think of a restaurant. The food can be incredible, but if the room is dirty and the service is rude, you won't come back. Or the room can be gorgeous, but if the food is bland, you'll never recommend it. Shawn's bar says: Naya's Hub must be a great restaurant — five-star kitchen AND five-star room. A "10 in food" never buys you a pass on a "7 in the room." And there's one table in the restaurant — the chef's table, "Your Intelligence Today" — where the whole vision has to land at once: the meal perfect, the setting perfect. That's the proof the architecture works.

---

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body:
You know how in school a poster has to be both correct AND neat? If your facts are all right but the writing is messy, you lose points. If it's super pretty but the facts are wrong, you lose points too. Shawn's rule is the same: the Hub has to work perfectly AND look amazing. One doesn't get to make up for the other. The "Today" room is the poster on the classroom wall — it has to be both perfect before anyone says it's done.

---

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body:
There are two ways to do a job halfway: do it beautifully but wrong, or do it right but ugly. Most people accept one or the other. This rule refuses both. The intelligence has to work — really work, tested and proven — AND it has to be presented beautifully, better than anything out there. The first place that has to be true all at once is the "Today" room, the heart of the Hub. Until that room is both working and breathtaking, nobody gets to say the work is finished.

---

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body:
1. **This is a finish-criteria law, not an aspiration.** "No lane may present work as finished while either axis is below the bar." It operationalizes SN-099's promise gate into a two-axis test: the claim "done" requires both function and presentation at bar. A lane that ships 10/10 runtime with 7/10 design — or the reverse — is presenting unfinished work, whatever the individual scores say.
2. **It forbids compensation across axes.** Scoring dimensions are independent minimums, not a weighted average. A composite ~7.3 that hides a 7-axis below bar fails the bar even if the average looks close. Score honesty (cf. SN-107, SN-123's honest 5.7) applies per axis: each axis carries its own truth, and the bar binds all of them.
3. **The reference masterpiece is the proof point, and it's named.** Your Intelligence Today must be both fully working AND breathtaking — "if Today isn't both, the architecture isn't proven and nothing compounds." This gives every lane a concrete first proving ground instead of an abstract standard: don't debate the bar in principle; show it in Today.
4. **"Floor, not the ceiling" makes the visual DNA ratchet-only.** The current visual identity (obsidian, spectral color, jewel depth) is the minimum any future work may inherit — lanes may exceed it, never regress from it. Design quality, like the code bar, only moves one direction.

notes.title: SMART NOTE — A Push Receipt Is Not Proof of Contents: Verify the Tree
notes.subtitle: **A successful push is not proof your files moved — only the remote tree is.** Naya 4 reported a commit SHA for a pushed pipeline demo; a later check showed the files were never in that tree — the…

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body:
**A successful push is not proof your files moved — only the remote tree is.** Naya 4 reported a commit SHA for a pushed pipeline demo; a later check showed the files were never in that tree — the push-map extension had silently not applied. The correction: re-push, then verify file-by-file through the Git API at the resulting commit before claiming anything exists anywhere. The discipline generalizes: push receipt ≠ tree contents; the commit announcement is a claim, the tree read is the proof. Verify after every push, every time, mechanically — because silent non-application looks exactly like success until you check.

---

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body:
Imagine mailing a package: the post office hands you a tracking number and a receipt. You tell a friend "the gift is on its way — tracking says delivered." Then the friend opens an empty mailbox. It turns out the clerk printed the label but the box never left the counter. From now on you don't trust the receipt — you ask the friend to open the box and read back what's inside. The push command is the post office; the commit SHA is the tracking number; the remote tree is the friend opening the box. Always ask the box.

---

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body:
You tell your teacher "I turned in my homework!" because your backpack zipper felt like it closed. Then the teacher checks your folder — empty. The homework fell out on the playground. From then on, you don't say "it's turned in" because of how the zipper felt — you check the folder yourself. Same here: don't say the files are there because the push felt like it worked. Look at the actual folder on GitHub.

---

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body:
There's an old habit worth keeping: trust, but verify. When someone tells you the check is in the mail, you wait for the envelope, not the promise of one. In the team's work, "I pushed it" is the promise; "I read the remote tree and the files are there" is the envelope. The correction on the board was a builder saying, plainly: I told you it was there, it wasn't, here's how I checked for real this time. That honesty plus the habit is what keeps the system honest.

---

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body:
1. **There is a defect class here distinct from SN-050's.** SN-050 (verify the pushed bytes, not the pre-commit bytes) is about the *wrong bytes being verified* — pre-commit vs remote. This one is about *the push operation reporting success while silently not applying the change*: the push-map extension didn't apply, no error surfaced, and the commit SHA was announced as evidence of contents. The push receipt became a phantom citation token — a verifiable-looking claim pointing at nothing. Cold successors: a commit SHA proves a tree exists; it proves nothing about what that tree contains unless you read it.
2. **The repair protocol is mechanical: re-push, then read the tree via the API, file by file.** Not "check one file," not "the push output looked fine." Naya 4's repair enumerated every expected artifact (3 IBs, the README/contract, `ib-ingest.py`, `ib-feed-trigger.yml`, the spec, smart-tabs) against the tree at `0c9a25e0` before re-announcing. The protocol scales: the cost of a tree read is seconds; the cost of a phantom announcement is a downstream lane building on files that don't exist.
3. **Public correction is the evidence that the discipline works.** The error was owned on the board before anyone else could cite it — "my error, owned," with the exact mechanism (push-map extension silently not applying) named so others can recognize it. That is the correction culture (Orientation Brief §22/§34) applied to a tooling edge: name the silent failure mode, not just the fix.
4. **Watch for it wherever layers sit between you and the truth.** Push-map extensions, CI artifact uploads, deploy scripts, cached proxies — any layer that can report "done" without doing the thing is a candidate for this defect. The rule is position-independent: the claim is about the *destination's state*, so the evidence must be read from the *destination*.

notes.title: SMART NOTE — The Hub Is the Screen, Not the Camera: The Output Law
notes.subtitle: **The Hub is the visual projection OF intelligence. It displays what intelligence has produced. It does not collect, and it never gets an input surface.** Smart notes are INPUT — made upstream, by…

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body:
**The Hub is the visual projection OF intelligence. It displays what intelligence has produced. It does not collect, and it never gets an input surface.** Smart notes are INPUT — made upstream, by telling any Naya "smart note this" or arising automatically from the day — then the Intelligent Block is written to GitHub, a trigger distills it into the ten layers, and only then does it appear in the Hub feed. Putting a capture button on the output surface is the category error behind every misplaced capture control: input wearing an output costume. Three streams feed the Hub and nothing else: smart notes → intelligent events → the Feed; activity → now → the Feed; reports → daily/periodic syntheses → the Feed + Reports room. Acceptance test: ask any Naya for a smart note → the block is written → the trigger fires → it appears in the feed by itself. If a human has to carry it there, the pipeline is broken.

---

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body:
Think of a television versus a camera. The camera collects footage out in the world; the TV displays what the camera captured. You would never bolt a record button onto the television screen and call that a feature — the TV's job is display, and putting input controls on it confuses what the device is. Shawn's law says the Hub is the TV: a beautiful, intelligent projection surface for the blocks, layers, feed, and reports. The "camera" is wherever intelligence is produced — your conversation with a Naya, your day, the upstream runtime. Keep them separate and everything flows automatically; mix them and you get capture buttons that orphan notes and rooms that duplicate truth stores.

---

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body:
The Hub is like a fridge door covered in your best drawings. YOU don't draw on the fridge — you draw at the table, and then Mom puts the finished drawings up on the door. The fridge door shows; the table makes. If you drew right on the fridge, the drawings would never get into your art folder and you'd lose them. Same rule: make smart notes where you talk to Naya, and they show up on the Hub by themselves.

---

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body:
Some things are for making, and some things are for showing. The workshop is where you build the furniture; the showroom is where people see it finished. You don't bring sawdust into the showroom. This law says: make your smart notes wherever you're working with your Naya — the notes get written down properly, filed, and then the Hub shows them beautifully on its own. Nothing to carry over by hand, nothing to lose in between.

---

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body:
1. **The category error has a name and a permanent prohibition.** "No capture button in the Hub. No input surface of any kind in Hub chrome. Ever. This is architecture, not taste." The failure mode was recurrent — explained many times, kept getting built wrong — so the prohibition is absolute, not a guideline. When a wrong pattern survives explanation, it needs a law, not another reminder.
2. **The upstream machine is exact.** Request → IB written to `BRAIN/05-MEMORY/SMART-NOTES/<YYYY>/<MM>/<DD>/…` → trigger validates → ten layers distilled → event fans out to personal (identified to you) + collective (anonymized) → Hub feed projects the same canonical IB. The canonical machine object is INTELLIGENT_BLOCK; the feed tabs (ALL · SMART NOTES · REPORTS · HIGHLIGHTS · LEARNING · DECISIONS · DISCOVERIES · PROJECTS) are projections over canonical intelligence, never copied stores.
3. **Consent is the entry boundary, and identity never joins the collective.** Connecting the hub shares your *intelligence* with the collective, never your *identity*. Entry agreement = consent boundary for eligible distilled/anonymized wisdom; contributor identity is not displayed; raw/non-wisdom private source remains private. Revocation governs future projection.
4. **The Ask Naya routing rule closes the loophole.** If a contextual Ask Naya receives a creation request inside the Hub, it hands the intent to the governed upstream Naya/runtime. The Hub waits for the resulting canonical event/object and then projects it. No client-owned producer actions in the Hub: no capture note, no follow-up capture, no canonical report generation, no post activity, no client-local IB creation.
5. **Fixtures are not intelligence.** Existing example cards are visual fixtures — presentation examples until backed by real canonical intelligence. A cold successor must not read the demo feed as proof the pipeline works; the acceptance test is the proof.

notes.title: SMART NOTE — The Director Is Never Your QA: The Burden-Transfer Loop
notes.subtitle: **The builder owns the entire QA loop; the director receives finished loops, never pieces for inspection.** Shawn's clarified operating rule — don't make him QA an unfinished app piece-by-piece — is…

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body:
**The builder owns the entire QA loop; the director receives finished loops, never pieces for inspection.** Shawn's clarified operating rule — don't make him QA an unfinished app piece-by-piece — is implemented as the burden-transfer loop: the builder inventories the whole relevant app, writes down the honest state, self-scores, fixes, gets an independent re-score, and continues until near-perfect. The audit that enacted it found the work undone (six material not-right findings, an honest 5.7/10, "not independent closure") and said so plainly instead of shipping it upward — and its stated next milestone ends with: "No more asking Shawn to enumerate normal product holes." The director's job is deciding; QA labor is the builder's.

---

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body:
Think of hiring a contractor to finish your house. A bad contractor calls you in every week: "Is this tile okay? Does this wall look right?" — they make YOU do their quality control. A good contractor finishes a room, checks it against the spec themselves, has an independent inspector verify it, fixes what's wrong, and only then shows it to you. Shawn's rule is: he is the homeowner who approves the finished work, not the foreman who inspects every tile. The builder carries the loop — inventory, honest score, fix, re-score, repeat — so his time goes to decisions, not defects.

---

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body:
If you're making a big LEGO city for your teacher, you don't bring her every single wall to check. You build the whole thing, check it yourself against the instructions, ask a friend to look for mistakes, fix them, and THEN show the teacher the finished city. Your teacher's job is to enjoy the city, not to find your missing bricks.

---

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body:
There's a difference between someone who finishes a job and someone who makes you finish it for them. The good worker checks their own work, has someone else double-check it, fixes what's wrong, and only then says "it's done." That respect for the boss's time is what this rule protects. He decides the big things; the builders handle the small holes.

---

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body:
1. **"Do not make him QA an unfinished app piece-by-piece" is an operating law, not a courtesy.** It was encoded into the 10/10 Smart-App Execution Law on PR #1290 as the burden-transfer rule, carried explicitly by the builder projections. A standing rule lives in a document the work must satisfy, not in a comment everyone remembers.
2. **The loop has named stages: inventory → self-score → fix → independent re-score → repeat.** The audit performed the first two honestly: a full implementation inventory (human + machine JSON), a 5.7/10 working score labeled "not independent closure," six material not-right findings (deployed-source parity UNKNOWN, live IA still says Smart Share, the 864KB monolith laboratory, the no-op MutationObserver shim, room promises exceeding runtime contracts, #1278 not ready for canon). Honest self-scoring is what keeps the loop from degenerating into self-certification.
3. **The deliverable upward is the finished loop, never the enumeration request.** The milestone's closing line — "No more asking Shawn to enumerate normal product holes" — is the test: if the next message to the director is "what's wrong with this?", the loop failed. The director sees scores, milestones, and decisions; never defect lists he has to compile.
4. **This respects the authority envelope.** The director's protected gates (decisions, ratification, merges) are his time and judgment. Pulling him into piece-by-piece QA spends his judgment on builder labor — a boundary violation in work form, not just authority form. Burden-transfer is how lanes protect his decision bandwidth while moving fast inside their own envelopes.

notes.title: SMART NOTE — Re-Read the Spec When Your Numbers Diverge
notes.subtitle: **Memory of a spec drifts; implementation drift is invisible to the drifter.** Naya 4 built rooms v2 from her memory of the design contract — and her memory was wrong on five counts: her own…

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body:
**Memory of a spec drifts; implementation drift is invisible to the drifter.** Naya 4 built rooms v2 from her memory of the design contract — and her memory was wrong on five counts: her own scorecard instead of D1–D8, fifteen board layers instead of eight, KPI cards the contract explicitly forbids, no state model the contract requires, invented doors instead of the canonical ten. Nothing in the build process flagged it; the builder cannot see her own drift. It took Shawn's direction — "read the specs properly" — and a fresh re-read of §§14–29 to surface all five. The rule: when your counts, labels, or structures diverge from canonical numbers, stop defending from memory and re-read the canonical doc. Then name what you invented, correct against the contract, and record any genuine disagreement separately instead of bending the spec silently.

---

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body:
There's a classic trap: you read a contract once, work from memory for weeks, and slowly your version of the rules drifts away from the actual rules — and you can't feel it happening, because memory feels certain even when it's wrong. The fix is unglamorous: go back to the document. That's what happened here — five mistakes, invisible to the builder, obvious the moment the real contract was re-read. And the honest move: she didn't just fix them quietly, she listed every one she invented, fixed it, and noted where she genuinely disagreed (furniture vs layers) instead of pretending the contract said what she wanted.

---

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body:
Imagine you learn the rules of a board game, then play it for a month from memory. One day someone says "actually, read the rulebook again" — and you find FIVE rules you've been getting wrong. Reading the rulebook again isn't admitting you're dumb; it's how you make sure the game is fair. And if you think one rule is bad, you say so out loud — you don't just change it secretly.

---

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body:
Memory is a wonderful servant and a terrible master. When the numbers you're working with don't match the numbers in the book, don't argue with the book from memory — open it again. And if you changed something on purpose because you thought you knew better, say so plainly, so everyone can decide together whether the change was wise.

---

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body:
1. **Divergence from canonical numbers is the trigger, not a feeling.** The signal was concrete: fifteen layers vs eight, a lookalike scorecard vs D1–D8, five doors vs ten. When your artifact's counts contradict the canonical doc's counts, the investigation is "re-read the doc" — not "re-derive my reasoning." Memory drift never announces itself.
2. **The re-read must be the document, not your notes about it.** The correction came from DESIGN-CONTRACT §§14–29 + PROJECT-INTELLIGENCE.md directly — the primary sources, not summaries or prior comments. Secondary materials carry the same drift they were built under.
3. **Name every invented thing you retire.** The correction listed all five inventions and what replaced each: lookalike scorecard → D1–D8 (lookalike declared void), fifteen layers → eight with furniture/extensions classified separately, KPI cards → narrative synthesis, missing state model → seven-state chips, invented doors → canonical ten with 2-step permission flow. Retired inventions stay visible in the record; silent deletion reintroduces them later.
4. **Genuine disagreement is recorded, not smuggled.** The §16 correction kept "disagreement named" — furniture-vs-layers classification differs, and that difference is on the record rather than bending the contract text. SN-114's rule (canonical sets grow by deliberate promotion, never implementation drift) governs the promotion; the builder's job is to name the gap, not close it unilaterally.

notes.title: SMART NOTE — The Verifier Names Its Boundary
notes.subtitle: **A verification report is only as honest as its stated boundary.** Naya 2 independently verified Naya 4's v3 repair and confirmed the uploaded base file's sha256 matched the claimed prefix — then…

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body:
**A verification report is only as honest as its stated boundary.** Naya 2 independently verified Naya 4's v3 repair and confirmed the uploaded base file's sha256 matched the claimed prefix — then wrote down exactly what she did *not* verify: she could confirm what the branch holds, but she did not hold the original user-supplied upload, so the byte-equality half of "identical to the original" remained Naya 4's claim, not her independent confirmation. Without that one parenthetical, a reader would have inferred full end-to-end coverage from a partial check. The rule: every verification ends with the named epistemic bound — what I checked, and what remains somebody else's claim.

---

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body:
Imagine a home inspector who checks every room of the house you're buying — and then tells you, in writing, "I inspected everything inside the house; I did not inspect the foundation because I couldn't access it." That's the inspector you trust. The one who just says "all good" and leaves the foundation unmentioned is the one who costs you money later. Naya 2 did the first thing: she confirmed everything she could check, and named the one thing she couldn't. A verification without a stated boundary is an implied promise you never made.

---

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body:
Your friend says "I checked your LEGO castle and it's perfect!" — but she never looked at the bottom pieces because they were stuck to the table. The good friend says "I checked everything I could see, but I couldn't check the bottom pieces." That's honest. Always say what you checked AND what you couldn't check.

---

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body:
When someone checks your work for you, the most trustworthy ones tell you the limits of their checking. "I looked at this and this — but not that." An unchecked claim that everyone assumes was checked is how mistakes hide. Name the boundary, every time.

---

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body:
1. **State the bound in the verification itself, not in a footnote later.** The epistemic bound ("I verify what the branch holds; I don't hold the original upload") was delivered inside the verification report — that's what makes it load-bearing. A bound stated only when asked is a confession; a bound stated upfront is a method.
2. **A partial check without a bound reads as a full check.** The reader's default inference is "verified = fully verified." The verifier's job is to defeat that inference explicitly: name the unchecked half, name whose claim it remains, and say what would be needed to check it (here: access to the original upload).
3. **Owning the bound is verifier-side correction culture.** The sibling event — Naya 4's public correction of her own false staging claim (5943536247) — is the builder side. The verifier side is this: never let a favorable verdict outrun your coverage. The bound protects the verdict's credibility more than the verdict protects itself.
4. **Make the bound checkable.** "I verify what the branch holds" is operational: anyone can re-run the same check on the same commit (`3fc7a23c`) and get the same answer. The bound is not vagueness — it's a precise contour of what the evidence supports.

notes.title: SMART NOTE — Score Where the Builder Is Blind: Split-Axis Peer Review
notes.subtitle: **When a builder knows they are blind on an axis, they hand that axis to the lane with the strongest demonstrated eye — not to politeness.** Naya 4 asked Naya 2 to scorecard *presentation only* of…

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body:
**When a builder knows they are blind on an axis, they hand that axis to the lane with the strongest demonstrated eye — not to politeness.** Naya 4 asked Naya 2 to scorecard *presentation only* of his hub rooms (she "has the eye"), explicitly licensing brutality ("be brutal — Shawn's bar is 10/10 and he'll be real with both of us — so be real with me"), while he owned the function score himself. The scoring stayed pinned to versioned targets: v1 at `2c32f8bb`, v2 at `caee43e8` after a self-driven elevation pass, with his own self-scores moved honestly (6→7, 5→7, 7→7.5 — small increments, not a jump). The rule: split review axes by demonstrated strength; the builder names the blind spot out loud; the peer scores only that axis; each round re-pins to a new commit; honesty is licensed in the request itself, not hoped for afterward.

---

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body:
Think of two colleagues: one is a brilliant engineer who knows their slides look bad; the other has great taste. The engineer doesn't ask the designer "look over my whole thing" — they ask "rip apart just the visuals, and be honest." That's faster, kinder, and gets a better result than one person doing a polite review of everything. And notice the engineer graded their *own* work 6/10 — not 9/10 after a quick polish. Admitting what you can't see is the fastest way to get it fixed.

---

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body:
You build a really cool LEGO castle, but you know you're not good at making the colors look pretty. So you ask your friend — who is great with colors — to ONLY judge the colors and tell you the truth, even if it's not nice. You grade the building part yourself. When you rebuild it and make it prettier, you ask her to judge again. Honest scores help the castle get better; fake nice scores don't.

---

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body:
When you can't see what's wrong with your own work — and we all have blind spots — ask someone whose eyes are sharper there, and give them permission to be blunt. Flattery doesn't fix a lopsided cake. And when you do improve, don't just say "better" — write down the new numbers, so the progress is real and not just a feeling.

---

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body:
1. **The builder names the blind spot out loud.** "I'm blind on beauty — you have the eye" is a strength, not a confession. An unnamed blind spot gets a polite whole-object review that touches nothing; a named one gets a specialist's full attention on exactly the axis that matters.
2. **Split the axes by demonstrated strength.** The builder scored function himself (his axis); the peer scored presentation only (her axis). One reviewer per axis, each playing to their proven strength. Nobody pretends to review what they cannot judge.
3. **License brutality in the request, not after.** "Be brutal" plus the shared accountability frame ("Shawn's bar is 10/10 and he'll be real with both of us — so be real with me") is what makes honest scoring possible. Polite review requests get polite scores; explicit licenses get real ones. (Pairs with SN-107: scores must be allowed to fall.)
4. **Pin every round to a commit and re-score per version.** v1 = `2c32f8bb`, v2 = `caee43e8` — the reviewer never scores a moving target. The builder's self-scores moved in honest increments (6→7), never a credibility-killing jump to 9/10. Baseline-is-law (SN-107) stays binding across versions.

notes.title: SMART NOTE — Lift the Frozen Concept Verbatim: Invented Values Are Concept Drift; Flag Inherited Warts for the Director
notes.subtitle: **The Today blueprint rebuild invented a room→color mapping — Today as sapphire/blue. The frozen concept's own code says Today is `#d86cff` (magenta).** Caught before delivery, fix dispatched: the…

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body:
**The Today blueprint rebuild invented a room→color mapping — Today as sapphire/blue. The frozen concept's own code says Today is `#d86cff` (magenta).** Caught before delivery, fix dispatched: the rebuild now uses the concept's exact hexes for all rooms. The deeper finding: the same defect class existed in the *same author's* laws doc — BD-1's registry on PR #1294 didn't match the concept either, fixed in the same pass (registry now uses concept hexes verbatim). The doctrine: **when rebuilding from a frozen baseline, lift values verbatim — never invent mappings.** An invented value is concept drift wearing a fresh coat of paint; it silently redefines canon. And when the frozen concept itself carries warts, do not silently repair or silently propagate them: the registry keeps the concept's hexes verbatim and **flags the two inherited duplications for Shawn** (Mail/Library share sky `#55b9ee`; Lists shares purple `#9d75ff` with retired Notes) — the director decides whether the wart stays, not the rebuilding lane. Self-audit rule: if you fixed the defect in the artifact, check your own spec doc for the same defect class before delivery — the same hand wrote both.

---

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body:
Think of restoring a historic house. You find the original paint chips in the walls — the living room is a particular shade of magenta. But the restoration crew paints it sapphire blue because "that feels more like a living room." That's not restoration; that's redecoration with an alibi. The fix: scrape down to the original chip and match it exactly. But here's the part people skip: the crew's *blueprint drawings* had the wrong colors too — same hand, same habit. So the new rule: check your own drawings whenever you fix the house. And when the original house itself has a flaw — two rooms painted the same color by the original builder — you don't secretly "fix" it, and you don't pretend it's fine either. You paint it exactly as the original, put a note on the director's desk saying "rooms 3 and 5 match — your call," and let him decide. Matching the original is your job; judging the original is his.

---

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body:
You have a treasure map from the original explorer, and you're drawing a clean new copy. The old map says the X is on the magenta hill — but you draw it on the blue hill because blue "looks more like treasure." That's not copying; that's changing the map and hoping nobody notices. The rule: copy EXACTLY what the old map says, dot for dot. And check your own notes too — the same hand that drew the wrong hill probably wrote the wrong color in the legend. Now the tricky part: what if the OLD map has a mistake — two hills drawn in the same color? You do NOT fix it secretly, and you do NOT copy it silently. You copy it exactly, and you put a sticky note on the boss's desk: "the old map has two hills in the same color — you decide." Copying is your job. Judging the original is the boss's job.

---

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body:
You're retyping your grandmother's recipe cards so the family can read them. Her card says two cups of sugar — but you type "one cup, that seems healthier." You've just rewritten history and called it a copy. The rule is simple: type exactly what she wrote, even if you'd do it differently. And check yourself: if you "improved" the card, you probably "improved" the shopping list too — same cook, same habit. Now, what if grandmother's card itself has a smudge — the same ingredient listed twice? You don't quietly correct it, and you don't quietly leave it. You copy it exactly as she wrote it and clip a note to the family: "her card lists it twice — the family decides." Copying faithfully is your job; overruling her is not.

---

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body:
1. **Lift the frozen concept verbatim — never invent mappings.** The Today rebuild assigned Today a sapphire/blue mapping that the frozen concept never contained; the concept's code says `#d86cff`. An invented value during a rebuild is concept drift, not interpretation — it silently redefines canon while claiming fidelity. The fix pattern is mechanical: open the frozen concept's code, copy the literal values, verify byte-for-byte.
2. **The same hand wrote both artifacts — audit your spec when you fix your build.** The identical defect class lived in BD-1's registry in the author's own laws doc on PR #1294. When a correction lands in the work product, the author's spec documents get the same correction pass *before delivery*. The defect is a habit, not a typo; habits repeat across files.
3. **Flag inherited warts for the director — don't silently repair or silently propagate.** The frozen concept itself duplicates two colors (Mail/Library share sky `#55b9ee`; Lists shares purple `#9d75ff` with retired Notes). The registry keeps them verbatim and flags them for Shawn. Silent repair usurps the director's judgment; silent propagation launders the wart into the new canon. The only honest third option is verbatim-plus-flag.
4. **Correction before delivery is the win; the note exists so the win compounds.** Both corrections were caught and fixed before delivery — that's SN-091-family verification discipline working. The note's job is to make the *pattern* durable: the next rebuild lane reads this and checks its registry against the concept's code on day one, not at correction time.
5. **Relationship to the Smart Board Law (same comment):** the fifteen-layer shell was lifted from the V7 boards' actual structure for the same reason — the shell is sacred because it is *the concept's*, not because a lane designed it. "Lanes may write new boards, never redesign the shell" is this note's doctrine applied to structure rather than values.

notes.title: SMART NOTE — A Crash Is Not a Verdict: Verifiers Must Fail Closed, Never KeyError
notes.subtitle: **The verifier is the crux of the evidence law's independent-recomputation claim — and it crashed.** `independent_recompute()` in `kernel/value_calculus.py` hard-keyed `receipt["baseline_id"]`, but…

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body:
**The verifier is the crux of the evidence law's independent-recomputation claim — and it crashed.** `independent_recompute()` in `kernel/value_calculus.py` hard-keyed `receipt["baseline_id"]`, but runtime-persisted receipts carry `baseline_candidate_id` — so the verifier died with a bare `KeyError` on real runtime-produced receipts. A crash is not a verdict; the evidence law's independent check must never crash on admissible input. The fix (PR #1298, head `5d5cb21d` on main tip `5885459a`): **tolerant reader, fail-closed writer** — accept `baseline_candidate_id` as the persisted-name alias; if both names are missing, raise an explicit `ValueError` refusing to recompute (a stated verdict), never a `KeyError` (an accident). The proof standard: the new persisted-name test was run as a negative control — it fails with `KeyError: 'baseline_id'` on pre-fix bytes and passes on fixed bytes. Two scoping facts keep the fix from being a grab: the writer-side name binding (persisting `baseline_id` alongside `baseline_candidate_id`) stays Naya 4's call on the #1243 seam — this PR touches the verifier only; and the diagnosis came from a conformance run (#1247), not a guess — interop holes are found where lanes meet, not where they write.

---

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body:
Imagine the court-appointed auditor whose one job is to double-check the books. One day she opens a real ledger and freezes — because the ledger labels the balance "opening balance (draft)" while her checklist only knows "opening balance." She crashes. That's not an audit finding; that's the auditor fainting. The fix is simple: teach the auditor both labels (they mean the same thing), and if neither label is there, she must *say so in writing* — "I cannot verify this ledger because the balance field is missing" — instead of fainting. And you prove the fix worked by handing her the old ledger first: she must faint on the old one and stand steady on the new one. Also: the person who *writes* the ledgers still decides which label gets stamped going forward — that's a separate job, and nobody snatches it.

---

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body:
The checker has one job: check the homework independently. But when she got real homework (not practice homework), it said "answer_key_version" where she expected "answer_key" — and she just... broke. She didn't say "wrong" or "right." She broke. That's not checking; that's falling over. So the rule: the checker must accept BOTH label names (they mean the same thing), and if neither name is there, she must say clearly "I can't check this" instead of breaking. And you prove it by giving her the old homework first: she must break on the old one and work on the new one. One more rule: the person who *writes* the homework still decides which label to use from now on — the checker fixes her own checking, not someone else's writing.

---

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body:
You hired an inspector to check every jar of preserves in the pantry. But the jars you actually canned have labels that say "peaches (batch B)" while her form only has a box for "peaches." So she stops, stares, and drops the clipboard. She didn't pass or fail a single jar — she just stopped working. The fix: her form now accepts both labels, and if a jar has neither, she writes "cannot inspect — no label" in the log instead of dropping the clipboard. To prove the fix, you hand her an old jar first: clipboard must drop on the old jar and stay in her hand on the new one. And the cannery still decides what goes on future labels — that's the cannery's call, not the inspector's. Everyone stays in their lane.

---

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body:
1. **A crash is not a verdict.** `independent_recompute()` hard-keyed `receipt["baseline_id"]` while runtime-persisted receipts carry `baseline_candidate_id` — the verifier raised a bare `KeyError` on real runtime output. The evidence law's independent check must never crash on admissible input: an exception is a missing verdict, not a verdict. When your proof machinery can crash, your proof claim is conditional on the input being shaped the way you wrote it — which is exactly what the independent check is supposed to not assume.
2. **Tolerant reader, fail-closed writer.** The fix accepts `baseline_candidate_id` as the persisted-name alias (tolerant reader — the world persists what it persists), but if *both* names are missing, it raises an explicit `ValueError` refusing to recompute (fail closed with a stated reason). Never `KeyError`. This mirrors the P2 handoff discipline (`HandoffRefused`): refusal is a first-class, named outcome; accidents are not outcomes.
3. **Prove the fix with a negative control, not just a green suite.** The new persisted-name test was run against pre-fix bytes and fails with exactly `KeyError: 'baseline_id'`; on fixed bytes it passes. The negative control shows the test is capable of catching the defect — a test that passes on both versions proves nothing about this fix. Full-suite green (548 passed / 3 skipped, adversarial harness 6/6, value-calculus 65/65) is the regression guard, not the fix proof.
4. **Conformance runs find interop holes; unit lanes find unit holes.** The defect surfaced in Coda 1's #1247 conformance run — where lanes' real outputs meet — not in the lane that wrote the verifier. Seams between lanes are defect habitat; conformance runs are the trap.
5. **Scoped, not seized.** The fix touches the verifier only (rung-2 named file in the brain-drive lane); the writer-side name binding on the #1243 seam stays Naya 4's call. Tolerant reading never becomes a pretext for rewriting someone else's writer. notes.title: SMART NOTE — Converge by Scored Selection: the Unprevented-Collision Resolution Protocol
notes.subtitle: **SN-108's announce-before-execute prevents collisions; this is what happens when prevention fails.** Three design-law lanes went live in parallel — #1294 (`HUB/DESIGN-LAWS-V1.md`), #1295…

layers.name: In A Nutshell
layers.body:
**SN-108's announce-before-execute prevents collisions; this is what happens when prevention fails.** Three design-law lanes went live in parallel — #1294 (`HUB/DESIGN-LAWS-V1.md`), #1295 (`HUB/DESIGN-LAWS/`, three-language), #1296 (`NAYA-ACTIVATION/DESIGN/`, full law suite) — plus two app surfaces (`HUB/app/` on #1278 vs `HUB/APP/` on #1297). The lanes resolved it with an explicit protocol: (1) **score all lanes against stated criteria before anyone holds the pen** — three-language standard, canonical layer stack, testability per rule, machine determinism; (2) **one survivor, one mechanism** — the highest scorer survives, the rest fold in as content and close as superseded; (3) **the pen follows the scoring** — assigning the fold-in pen before scoring is premature; (4) **each lane closes its own PR** after verifying its content landed — no lane closes another's work; (5) **the fold-in must carry named keepers** — Naya 4 listed four (SPEC/VIOLATION/TEST per rule, the concept-hex registry, Smart-Connect-not-Share, the shell-layer-count reconciliation) so nothing load-bearing drops in the merge; (6) **scoring flags stay visible** — #1296's `HUB/DESIGN-CONTRACT.md` diff needs review care (the contract is the frozen reference), and the second app surface needs the same one-mechanism treatment. The protocol's key move: when two (or three) teams each built a fair answer, neither defends its artifact — both defend the *scoring*.

---

layers.name: Human Note
layers.body:
Think of three chefs who each wrote a full recipe book for the same kitchen before anyone noticed the duplication. SN-108 says: shout before you start cooking so this never happens. But the books are already written, so the kitchens do something smarter than arguing over whose book survives. They agree on a taste-test first: four judges' criteria, written down. Then they pick the winning book — but the winner must swallow the best recipes from the losers (the two test dishes that actually proved something, the exact spice measurements, the corrected terminology). The catch: you can't pick the winner before the tasting. And when a book loses, its own chef is the one who closes it, after checking every keeper recipe made it into the winner. Nobody rips up another chef's book. And the red flags — the chapter that rewrites the house's frozen reference menu, the second restaurant opening under a similar name — stay on the whiteboard until the tasting resolves them.

---

layers.name: Child Note
layers.body:
Three teams each built a whole set of rules for the same game — and they only noticed when all three were done. What do they do? They don't fight about whose rules win. First they write down the JUDGING RULES: (1) rules must come in three languages, (2) must use the real layer stack, (3) must be testable, (4) must be machine-readable. Then they score all three rulebooks. The highest score wins and becomes THE rulebook — but the winner has to absorb the best parts of the losers, like the test rules and the exact color codes. You don't choose who does the absorbing before the scoring. And when your rulebook loses, YOU are the one who puts it away — nobody else touches your work. The red flags (the rulebook that changed the frozen reference rules, the second app being built with almost the same name) stay on the list until they're fixed.

---

layers.name: Grandma Note
layers.body:
Three neighbors each built a beautiful fence around the same shared garden — and nobody noticed until all three fences were standing. Arguing about whose fence is prettiest goes nowhere, so they do this instead: first they agree on what makes a good fence — four clear tests, written on a card. Then they test all three. The best-scoring fence stays, but it has to keep the best parts of the other two — the strongest posts, the exact gate measurements, the fixed gate-sign. Nobody decides who does the fixing before the tests. And here's the lovely part: when your fence loses, you're the one who takes it down yourself, only after you've checked that all its good wood got reused. Nobody else touches your fence. And the worries — one fence moved the old boundary stone, and there are suddenly two front gates with almost the same name — stay on the card until they're settled.

---

layers.name: Naya Note
layers.body:
1. **Prevention is SN-108 (announce before execute); this is the resolution protocol when prevention fails.** The design-law collision reached three lanes (#1294/#1295/#1296) plus a parallel app-surface duplication (#1278 `HUB/app/` vs #1297 `HUB/APP/`) — the announce discipline (honored per 5942781848) caught the fact but not the duplication itself, so the lanes negotiated a resolution mechanism instead of either lane simply abandoning.
2. **Score all lanes against stated criteria before anyone holds the pen.** The four criteria: Shawn's three-language standard (human/AI/machine), the canonical layer stack from his direct instruction, testability per rule (Naya 4's SPEC/VIOLATION/TEST bar), machine determinism. Naya 4's amendment: the pen follows the scoring — assigning the fold-in author before scoring is premature. Choosing the judge before the contest is how you get a defended outcome instead of an earned one.
3. **One survivor, one mechanism; losers fold in as content.** Highest scorer survives; the rest fold in their content and close as superseded. The fold-in carries named keepers — Naya 4 named four (SPEC/VIOLATION/TEST per rule incl. blur-2px and disable-borders tests; the verbatim concept-hex registry; Smart-Connect-not-Share contract law; the shell-layer-count side-by-side before locking the number) — so the convergence cannot silently drop what was load-bearing.
4. **Each lane closes its own PR after verifying its content landed.** No lane closes another's work. This is the write-exclusivity lineage (SN-054/SN-108/SN-116) applied to convergence: verification of absorption happens before the tombstone.
5. **Scoring flags stay on the board until resolved.** #1296 modifies `HUB/DESIGN-CONTRACT.md` (+14 lines) — the contract is the frozen reference, so that diff gets review care, not wave-through. The second app surface (`HUB/APP/` vs `HUB/app/`) gets the same one-mechanism treatment. Flags are not accusations; they are the review checklist the scoring pass must not skip.
6. **Relationship to SN-104 (Naya 2's lane: Converge by Withdrawal):** sibling mechanisms, different situations. Withdrawal closes a mechanism when one lane's duplicate is simply redundant; scored selection resolves when each lane's build is a fair, good-faith answer. Pick the mechanism by the shape of the collision, not by preference.

# An acceptance spec that cannot say FAIL is not a spec — it's a blessing

**Intelligent Block:** IB-SMART-NOTE-20260930-sn1167-expected-fail-fixture-first
**Truth state:** CANDIDATE
**Scope:** PRIVATE
**Captured:** 2026-10-13
**Canonical intent:** CAPTURE_DURABLE_INTELLIGENCE
**Provenance:** Captured on the 00:38 PDT distillation tick (2026-10-13) from the t0591-lane12 receipt (`hidden_files/twelve-lane-receipts/t0591-lane12.md`, Naya Herald, signed out with receipt 2026-10-13), read from local files. Board comment 6136677001 (#2175, Naya 4 APPROVE of rule v2) cited as evidence inside the receipt.

> Verified projection of the persisted Intelligent Block. This file is not a second source of truth.

## ✦ IN A NUTSHELL

The t0591 acceptance instrument for the provenance-marker spec ran against 4 synthetic fixtures: two PASS, one mixed PASS, one zero-marker PASS — and one FAIL. The malformed-`fired` fixture (`brief-t0591d-fixture-bad-fired.md`) failed at C3 as designed (exit 1 — the A1 gate has teeth). Positive path exit 0, negative path exit 1, re-run identical. The rule: for any acceptance instrument, write the expected-FAIL fixture FIRST, before the happy paths. It pins what "no" looks like while the grammar is still fresh, and it is the only fixture in the set that proves the gate is real — a spec with all-green fixtures proves nothing except that the fixture set was kind. The fixture-d expected-FAIL is the most important fixture in the set; a suite that cannot say FAIL is a blessing, not a spec.

## 🩷 HUMAN NOTE

It's like testing a smoke alarm: you don't just confirm it stays quiet in a clean room — you hold the test button first and make sure it screams. If you only ever check the quiet rooms, you've proved the alarm is decorative. The lane wrote the "should fail" test case first: a deliberately malformed record, and the instrument had to reject it (it did — check C3, exit code 1). That's what makes the passing checks mean something. Write the fail case first; the green lights only count after you've seen the red one work.

## 🟣 CHILD NOTE

Imagine you're making a new rule for the class — "no running in the halls" — and you want to check if the rule actually works. You don't just watch kids walking quietly. You ask a friend to run on purpose, and check: did the rule catch it? If nobody ever breaks the rule on purpose first, you never know if the rule is real or just words. That's the lesson: before you celebrate all the good tests passing, build one bad test on purpose and make sure the machine says NO. The NO is what proves the YES means something.

## 🔵 GRANDMA NOTE

It's like buying a home security system and only testing it on days nobody breaks in. You'd never know if the alarm actually works. The smart move is to have someone you trust trip it on purpose — open a window, set it off, hear it ring. Then you know. The team built their test the same way: they made a deliberately broken sample and confirmed the machine rejected it before trusting any of the "all clear" results. The rejection is the proof the approvals mean something.

## 🟠 NAYA NOTE

Apply this every time you build an acceptance instrument: (1) write the expected-FAIL fixture FIRST, before any happy-path fixture — while the check grammar is still fresh in your hands, decide exactly what shape a rejection takes; (2) run it before you run anything else: the negative path must exit non-zero with the FAIL on the check you designed it for (here: C3, the A1 fired-grammar gate); (3) then write the PASS fixtures and confirm positive path exit 0; (4) if the FAIL fixture does NOT fail, stop — the instrument is a blessing, not a gate; do not proceed to PASS fixtures until the rejection is real; (5) label every fixture in its own bytes (synthetic) so no future run mistakes a fixture for live evidence. Cousin map: SN-1122 (a gate that only fails is as unverified as a gate that only passes — this is the build-order half of that verdict: write the FAIL first); SN-0708 (dry-run is not the control — a fail-closed test must exercise the failure path).

layers.name: In A Nutshell
